title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Previously

Bayesian inference

The parameter \(\theta\) is a random variable - probabilities describe our beliefs about it
Target of inference: the posterior \(f(\theta | \mathbf{Y}) \propto f(\mathbf{Y} | \theta) \times f(\theta)\)
Conjugate priors give posteriors with a closed form: Beta prior + Binomial likelihood \(\leadsto\) Beta posterior

Application: absentee ballot rejection in Wisconsin

Raw rejection rates (the MLE) in small municipalities are mostly noise
Pooling each municipality toward the statewide rate predicted better.

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Connections with Frequentism

In our earlier example, under an uninformative uniform prior, the posterior mode is equivalent to the MLE

If \(f(\theta) \propto 1\), \(f(\theta|\mathbf{Y}) \propto f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta)\)

More generally, for most well-behaved priors and likelihoods, the Bernstein-von Mises theorem states that as \(n \to \infty\)…

…the posterior distribution \(f(\theta | \mathbf{Y})\) will converge to a normal distribution
…centered at the MLE \(\hat{\theta}\) (which is itself converging to the true parameter \(\theta_0\))
…with variance-covariance matrix equal to the inverse Fisher information

Essentially: In large samples, posterior distributions converge to the sampling distribution of the MLEs

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
This week

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)

Most posteriors don’t have a closed form
Define an algorithm to draw samples from the posterior without knowing it directly.
The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm + Gibbs sampling

Introduction to Stan

Write down the model
Let Stan implement the MCMC sampler (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text: Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo

In many settings, we have this problem in computing the posterior
\[f(\theta | \mathbf{Y}) = \frac{\overbrace{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta)}^{\text{Easy!}} \times \overbrace{f(\theta)}^{\text{Easy!}}}{\underbrace{f(\mathbf{Y})}_{\textbf{HARD!}}}\]
The prior \(f(\theta)\) has a known distribution (sometimes up to a proportionality constant)
The likelihood \(f(\mathbf{Y} | \theta)\) has a known distribution specified by our data-generating process

We write our model so that the joint density \(f(\mathbf{Y}, \theta) = f(\mathbf{Y} | \theta) f(\theta)\) factors neatly

But \(f(\mathbf{Y})\) is a tough integral to evaluate!
\[f(\mathbf{Y}) = \int f(\mathbf{Y},\theta)d\theta\]
Last week we used a conjugate prior, which told us the form of the posterior without ever computing \(f(\mathbf{Y})\)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo

Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods generate a sample from the target posterior even when we don’t know it

All we need is a function that is proportional to the posterior
Monte Carlo: Use repeated samples to obtain numeric approximations of key quantities
Markov Chain: The samples are constructed via a chain that has the Markov property

Our Goal: Generate a Monte Carlo sample \(\{\theta^{(1)}, \theta^{(2)}, \theta^{(3)}, \dotsc \}\) of arbitrary length

The sequence of draws should converge to a stationary distribution that is the target posterior

This sample is a Markov chain: the distribution of the \((i+1)\)th draw depends on the \(i\)th, but only on that past value
\[f(\theta^{(i+1)} | \mathbf{Y},  \theta^{(i)}, \theta^{(i-1)}, \dotsc, \theta^{(1)}) =  f(\theta^{(i+1)} | \mathbf{Y},  \theta^{(i)})\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm

The foundational MCMC algorithm is Metropolis-Hastings (Metropolis et al. 1953; Hastings 1970). To generate a Markov chain of \(M\) samples \(\{\theta^{(1)}, \theta^{(2)}, \dotsc, \theta^{(M)}\}\), it iterates between two steps:


Proposal: Conditional on the current value \(\theta\), generate a draw \(\theta^*\) from the proposal distribution \(Q(\theta^* | \theta)\) – almost any distribution works (though some are better than others)
Accept/Reject: With acceptance probability \(\alpha\), “accept” the proposal and set \(\theta^{(i+1)} = \theta^*\) - otherwise “reject” and set \(\theta^{(i+1)} = \theta\)

\[\alpha = \min\bigg\{1, \frac{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta^*)f(\theta^*)}{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta)f(\theta)} \times \frac{Q(\theta | \theta^*)}{Q(\theta^* | \theta)} \bigg\}\]

Intuitively - If the proposal distribution is symmetric…

…if the unnormalized posterior density is higher at the proposed rather than the current location, always accept
…if the unnormalized posterior density is lower at the proposed rather than current location, maybe accept
Note that \(f(\mathbf{Y})\) would appear in both the numerator and the denominator – it cancels!

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm

To get some intuition, consider the case where somehow we could generate independent samples from the true posterior
\[Q(\theta^*|\theta) = f(\theta^* | \mathbf{Y})\]
What is our acceptance probability in this scenario?
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta^*)f(\theta^*)}{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta)f(\theta)} \times \frac{f(\theta|\mathbf{Y})}{f(\theta^*|\mathbf{Y})} = \frac{f(\theta^*|\mathbf{Y})f(\mathbf{Y})}{f(\theta|\mathbf{Y})f(\mathbf{Y})} \times \frac{f(\theta|\mathbf{Y})}{f(\theta^*|\mathbf{Y})} = 1\]
If we were somehow proposing from the true posterior distribution, Metropolis-Hastings would always accept each proposal!

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Proposal Distribution

Our choice of \(Q\) governs how quickly the Markov Chain will “converge” to the true posterior

We want a proposal distribution that could “eventually” propose each value in the domain of \(\theta\)
We also want a proposal distribution that generates a high acceptance probability \(\alpha\)

It is common to choose a proposal distribution that is symmetric such that \[\frac{Q(\theta | \theta^*)}{Q(\theta^* | \theta)} = 1\]
For \(\theta \in (-\infty, \infty)\), it’s common to propose \(\theta^*\) from a \(\text{Normal}(\theta, \Omega)\)

A normal distribution centered on the “current” parameter with an arbitrarily chosen variance \(\Omega\)
This is symmetric: the chances of proposing \(\theta^*\) from \(\theta\) are the same as the chances of proposing \(\theta\) from \(\theta^*\)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Proposal Distribution

Another alternative would be a \(\text{Uniform}(\theta - \Delta, \theta + \Delta)\)

Uniform distribution centered at \(\theta\) where every value in the interval has density \(\frac{1}{2\Delta}\)

For parameters that are constrained to \((0, 1)\), a simple choice would be to sample from the \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\)

Trivially symmetric since the density is a constant.
But likely to generate bad proposals!

A random walk still works for a constrained parameter

Proposals outside \((0, 1)\) have posterior density \(0\), so they are always rejected

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

Let’s go back to the absentee ballot data. Load it in just as we did last week


# EAVS 2024, Wisconsin municipalities (see data/README.md)
wi <- read_csv("data/eavs_2024_wi.csv")
wi <- wi %>% mutate(n = C1b - C9b - C9m, y = C9a - C9b - C9m) %>% # Discretionary rejections only
  filter(n > 0) %>% # Drop municipalities where no absentee ballots were returned
  transmute(FIPSCode, municipality = Jurisdiction_Name, n, y, mle = y/n)
state_rate <- sum(wi$y)/sum(wi$n)


And pull out the City of Mequon


mequon <- wi %>% filter(municipality == "CITY OF MEQUON - OZAUKEE COUNTY")
mequon

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  FIPSCode municipality                        n     y     mle
  <chr>    <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 51150    CITY OF MEQUON - OZAUKEE COUNTY  3978    34 0.00855

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

Use last week’s prior: centered on the rejection rate in the rest of the state, equivalent to 500 ballots


others_rate <- wi %>% filter(municipality != mequon$municipality) %>% summarize(rate = sum(y)/sum(n)) %>% pull(rate)
prior_alpha <- others_rate*500
prior_beta <- (1 - others_rate)*500


The Beta prior is conjugate, so we know the posterior exactly


posterior_alpha <- mequon$y + prior_alpha
posterior_beta <- mequon$n - mequon$y + prior_beta
ggplot() + xlim(0, .02) + geom_function(fun=dbeta, args=list(shape1=posterior_alpha, shape2=posterior_beta), n=1001) +
  theme_bw() + xlab(expression(pi)) + ylab("Density")



But suppose we couldn’t calculate it directly?

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

Let’s construct our MCMC sampler. First, let’s choose a proposal distribution

For \(\pi \in (0, 1)\), we could use a Beta, but the Beta isn’t symmetric
\(\text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) would generate a lot of bad proposals: the posterior is concentrated around \(.008\)

Instead, use a random walk: propose \(\pi^* \sim \text{Normal}(\pi, s^2)\), centered on the current value

It’s symmetric, so the \(Q\) terms cancel
The step size \(s\) is chosen by the researcher: too small and the chain explores the posterior little-by-little, too large and most proposals are rejected
If \(\pi^*\) falls outside \((0, 1)\), its posterior density is \(0\): we always reject it

We’ll also work with the log of the likelihood and prior

Products of many small densities can underflow to \(0\) – sums of logs won’t

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

set.seed(53706)
M <- 50000  # Number of MCMC samples
pi_mcmc <- rep(NA, M) # Vector to store our samples
pi_mcmc[1] <- .5 # Pick a starting value
step_sd <- .003 # Standard deviation of the random-walk proposal
# The log of the unnormalized posterior: log likelihood + log prior
log_post <- function(p){
  if (p <= 0 | p >= 1) return(-Inf) # Zero posterior density outside (0, 1)
  dbinom(mequon$y, mequon$n, prob = p, log=T) + # Log likelihood
    dbeta(p, shape1 = prior_alpha, shape2 = prior_beta, log=T) # Log prior
}

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

for (i in 1:(M-1)){ # For i in 1:(M-1)
  ## Step 1 - Proposal
  pi_star <- rnorm(1, mean = pi_mcmc[i], sd = step_sd)
  ## Step 2 - Accept/Reject
  log_post_star <- log_post(pi_star)
  log_post_current <- log_post(pi_mcmc[i])
  log_Q_star_current <- dnorm(pi_star, mean = pi_mcmc[i], sd = step_sd, log=T) # This is all optional b/c of symmetry
  log_Q_current_star <- dnorm(pi_mcmc[i], mean = pi_star, sd = step_sd, log=T)
  # Assemble the acceptance ratio (exponentiate the difference in logs)
  ar <- exp(log_post_star - log_post_current + log_Q_current_star - log_Q_star_current)
  # Choose to accept or reject
  accept <- rbinom(1, 1, min(1, ar))
  # Store the next value
  pi_mcmc[i+1] <- pi_star*accept + pi_mcmc[i]*(1-accept)
}


What share of proposals did we accept?


mean(diff(pi_mcmc) != 0)

[1] 0.453

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

Let’s first see how the chain progresses by generating the trace plot (the first 600 iterations)


plot(y=pi_mcmc[1:600], x=1:600, xlab="Iteration", ylab="pi", type="l")



The chain starts at \(.5\) and takes about 388 iterations to reach the area of the posterior with the most mass

If we started closer to the “mass” of the distribution, we would have converged faster

In practice, we will throw away some number of our initial samples as a burn-in period

The chain needs some time to reach the stationary distribution
Here we’ll drop the first \(1000\) samples and keep the rest

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

Our ideal trace plots have no clear trends - in such a case, we consider the chain to have reached its stationary distribution


pi_mcmc_use <- pi_mcmc[1001:M] # Toss our burn-in period
plot(y=pi_mcmc_use, x=1:length(pi_mcmc_use), xlab="Iteration", ylab="pi", type="l")



Trace plots are diagnostics: they can’t prove that the chain has “mixed”

But a lot of jumps or stagnant periods would suggest that our chain needs to run longer…
…or that we need a better proposal distribution!

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

The MCMC draws (histogram) against the exact Beta posterior (red)


# Plot the histogram on top of the "true" distribution
data.frame(x=pi_mcmc_use) %>% ggplot(aes(x=x)) + theme_bw() + xlab(expression(pi)) + ylab("Density") +
  geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat(density)), bins=50) +
  geom_function(fun=dbeta, args=list(shape1=posterior_alpha, shape2=posterior_beta), col="indianred", lwd=2)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Illustration

We can compute summaries like the posterior mean or a 95% credible interval by taking summaries of the MCMC sample


mean(pi_mcmc_use) # MCMC

[1] 0.00781

posterior_alpha/(posterior_alpha + posterior_beta) # Exact

[1] 0.00782



We get very close to the true posterior (and can get closer with more iterations)


quantile(pi_mcmc_use, c(.025, .975)) # MCMC

   2.5%   97.5% 
0.00543 0.01057 

qbeta(c(.025, .975), shape1=posterior_alpha, shape2=posterior_beta) # Exact

[1] 0.00545 0.01060

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Multiple parameters

In this example, we’ve focused on estimating a single parameter

Suppose instead we have \(K\) parameters: \(\theta = \{\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3, \dotsc, \theta_K\}\)

With multiple parameters, we’d need a multivariate proposal distribution (like a multivariate normal)

But this can be hard and mixing is often very slow with multivariate proposals.

Instead, we can use Gibbs sampling (Geman and Geman 1984; Gelfand and Smith 1990)

Generate each update \(\theta^{(i+1)}_k\) conditional on the current values of the other parameters \(\theta_{-k}\)
If we can sample from the conditional distribution \(\theta_k | \theta_{-k}, \mathbf{Y}\) we get proposals with acceptance probability 1
Even if we can’t, we can use a M-H step for that parameter (“Metropolis-within-Gibbs”)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Gibbs Sampling

The Gibbs sampling algorithm generates updates \(\theta^{(i+1)} = \{\theta^{(i+1)}_1, \theta^{(i+1)}_2, \theta^{(i+1)}_3, \dotsc, \theta^{(i+1)}_K\}\) by sampling in sequence:

\[\begin{align*}\theta_1^{(i+1)} &:= \theta^*_1 \sim f(\theta_1 | \mathbf{Y}, \theta_2^{(i)}, \theta_3^{(i)}, \dotsc \theta_K^{(i)})\\
\theta_2^{(i+1)} &:= \theta^*_2 \sim f(\theta_2 | \mathbf{Y}, \theta_1^{(i+1)}, \theta_3^{(i)}, \dotsc \theta_K^{(i)})\\
&\vdots\\
  \theta_k^{(i+1)} &:= \theta^*_k \sim f(\theta_k | \mathbf{Y}, \theta_1^{(i+1)}, \theta_2^{(i+1)}, \dotsc \theta_{k-1}^{(i+1)},\theta_{k+1}^{(i)} \dotsc, \theta_K^{(i)})\\
   &\vdots\\
  \theta_K^{(i+1)} &:= \theta^*_K \sim f(\theta_K | \mathbf{Y}, \theta_1^{(i+1)}, \theta_2^{(i+1)}, \dotsc \theta_{K-1}^{(i+1)})\end{align*}\]

Important: Sampling from the conditionals \(f(\theta_k | \theta_{-k}, \mathbf{Y})\) is often easier than sampling from the marginal \(f(\theta_k | \mathbf{Y})\).

We’ll often introduce latent variables to make a Gibbs sampler work where it otherwise wouldn’t. This is called data augmentation

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Gibbs Sampling

To see why sampling from the conditionals works, treat the conditional distribution \(f(\theta_{k} | \theta_{-k}^{(i)} , \mathbf{Y})\) as the proposal distribution \(Q\). The implied MH acceptance probability is

\[\alpha = \frac{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta^*_k, \theta^{(i)}_{-k})f(\theta^*_k, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}{f(\mathbf{Y}|\theta^{(i)}_k, \theta^{(i)}_{-k})f(\theta^{(i)}_k, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})} \times \frac{f(\theta^{(i)}_k|\mathbf{Y}, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}{f(\theta^{*}_k|\mathbf{Y}, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}\]

Rewrite the numerator/denominator in terms of the posterior and the data (and recall that \(f(\mathbf{Y})\) cancels)

\[\alpha = \frac{f(\theta^*_k, \theta^{(i)}_{-k}|\mathbf{Y})}{f(\theta^{(i)}_k, \theta^{(i)}_{-k}|\mathbf{Y})} \times \frac{f(\theta^{(i)}_k|\mathbf{Y}, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}{f(\theta^{*}_k|\mathbf{Y}, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Gibbs Sampling

Factor the posteriors

\[\alpha = \frac{f(\theta^*_k| \theta^{(i)}_{-k},\mathbf{Y}) \times f(\theta^{(i)}_{-k}|\mathbf{Y})}{f(\theta^{(i)}_k | \theta^{(i)}_{-k}, \mathbf{Y}) \times f(\theta^{(i)}_{-k}|\mathbf{Y})} \times \frac{f(\theta^{(i)}_k|\mathbf{Y}, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}{f(\theta^{*}_k|\mathbf{Y}, \theta_{-k}^{(i)})}\]

Everything cancels so that \(\alpha = 1\)

So Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings where the proposal distribution choice guarantees acceptance.

But, we need to know the conditional distributions \(f(\theta_k | \theta_{-k}, \mathbf{Y})\)

This is where conjugacy comes back in!

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text: Bayesian Regression

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Bayesian Normal Model

The conventional “normal” Bayesian regression model assumes
\[Y_i | X_i, \beta, \sigma^2 \sim \text{Normal}(X_i^{\prime}\beta, \sigma^2)\] \[\beta | \sigma^2 \sim \text{Normal}(b_0, \sigma^2B^{-1}_0)\] \[\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inverse-Gamma}\left(\frac{c_0}{2}, \frac{d_0}{2}\right)\]
\(b_0\), \(B_0\), \(c_0\) and \(d_0\) are all hyperparameters
This is the “Normal-Inverse-Gamma” model: the joint prior on \(\beta, \sigma^2\) is Normal-Inverse-Gamma

It is also the conjugate prior for the normal regression with unknown \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\)
So the posterior is known in closed form to be Normal-Inverse-Gamma

A common simplification is to make \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) marginally independent
\[\beta \sim \text{Normal}(b_0, B_0^{-1})\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Plate notation


With independent priors, there is no arrow from \(\sigma^2\) to \(\beta\)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Aside: Conditional distributions

To build a Gibbs sampler for \(f(\beta, \sigma^2 | \mathbf{Y})\), we need the conditionals \(f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2)\) and \(f(\sigma^2 | \mathbf{Y}, \beta)\).

Can we derive them (or at least their distributional forms?)

Deriving these conditionals often relies on inspecting a density that is proportional to the conditional density and recognizing its form.

Remember the connection between conditional and joint densities, as well as how joint densities factor.

From the definition of a conditional density: joint divided by marginal
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) = \frac{f(\beta, \sigma^2 | \mathbf{Y})}{f(\sigma^2 | \mathbf{Y})}\]
Since we treat \(\sigma^2\) here as a constant, we can write
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) \propto f(\beta, \sigma^2 | \mathbf{Y}) \propto f(\mathbf{Y} | \beta, \sigma^2)f(\beta, \sigma^2)\]
where the last part follows from Bayes’ rule

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Aside: Conditional distributions

Next, remember how distributions factor
\[f(\beta, \sigma^2) = f(\beta | \sigma^2)f(\sigma^2)\]
If \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\) are marginally independent, then the joint distribution factors into the marginals

But even if they’re not independent, we can always factor into a product of conditionals

So we have
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) \propto f(\mathbf{Y} | \beta, \sigma^2)f(\beta | \sigma^2) f(\sigma^2)\]
Again, \(\sigma^2\) is a constant here, so that last density drops as a multiplicative constant
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) \propto f(\mathbf{Y} | \beta, \sigma^2)f(\beta | \sigma^2)\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Aside: Conditional distributions

With independent priors, \(f(\beta | \sigma^2) = f(\beta)\)
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) \propto f(\mathbf{Y} | \beta, \sigma^2)f(\beta)\]
And independence of observations gives
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) \propto \bigg[\prod_{i=1}^N f(Y_i | \beta, \sigma^2)\bigg]f(\beta)\]
The key is finding densities that are given by our model description - now all of these factors are known
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2) \propto \bigg[\prod_{i=1}^N \underbrace{f(Y_i | \beta, \sigma^2)}_{\text{Normal}(X_i^{\prime}\beta, \sigma^2)}\bigg]\times\underbrace{f(\beta)}_{\text{Normal}(b_0, B_0^{-1})}\]
One useful property from probability theory: the product of two normal PDFs is proportional to a normal PDF

So \(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \sigma^2\) is normal!

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Normal-normal conjugacy

The algebra is cleaner in terms of the precision \(\tau^2 = 1/\sigma^2\) rather than the variance
To see why the normal is conjugate to the normal, plug in the densities and drop multiplicative constants
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \tau^2) \propto \bigg[\prod_{i=1}^N \exp\bigg(-\frac{\tau^2}{2}(Y_i - X_i^\prime \beta)^2\bigg)\bigg]\times \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}(\beta - b_0)^{\prime}B_0(\beta - b_0)\bigg)\]
A product of exponentials is the exponential of a sum. Write the sum of squares in matrix form
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \tau^2) \propto \exp\bigg(-\frac{\tau^2}{2}(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\beta)^\prime (\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\beta)\bigg)\times \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}(\beta - b_0)^\prime B_0(\beta - b_0)\bigg)\]
Expand both quadratic forms and drop the terms that don’t involve \(\beta\) (they’re constants)
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \tau^2) \propto \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}\bigg[\beta^\prime \big(\tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime \mathbf{X}\big)\beta - 2\beta^\prime \tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime \mathbf{Y} \bigg]\bigg)\times \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}\bigg[\beta^\prime B_0\beta - 2\beta^\prime B_0 b_0\bigg]\bigg)\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Normal-normal conjugacy

Collect terms
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \tau^2) \propto \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}\bigg[\beta^\prime \big(B_0 + \tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime \mathbf{X}\big)\beta - 2\beta^\prime \big(B_0 b_0 + \tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime \mathbf{Y}\big) \bigg]\bigg)\]
“Completing the square”: call the matrix in the first term \(V^{-1}\) and write the vector in the second as \(V^{-1}\mu\)
\[\beta^\prime V^{-1}\beta - 2\beta^\prime V^{-1}\mu = (\beta - \mu)^\prime V^{-1}(\beta - \mu) - \mu^\prime V^{-1}\mu\]

The last term doesn’t involve \(\beta\), so it drops out

\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}, \tau^2) \propto \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{2}(\beta - \mu)^\prime V^{-1}(\beta - \mu)\bigg)\]
We recognize this as the kernel of a multivariate normal with variance-covariance matrix \(V\) and mean \(\mu\)
\[V = \big(B_0 + \tau^2\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\mathbf{X}\big)^{-1}, \qquad \mu = V\big(B_0b_0 + \tau^2\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\mathbf{Y}\big)\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Normal-normal conjugacy

The posterior precision \(V^{-1} = B_0 + \tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}\) is the prior precision plus the precision from the data

The mean is a precision-weighted combination of the prior mean \(b_0\) and the data
Just like the Beta-Binomial: the weight on the prior shrinks as \(N\) grows

As \(N \to \infty\), \(\tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}\) swamps \(B_0\)…

…so \(\mu \to (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{Y}\) (OLS!) and \(V \to (\tau^2\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\)

The same steps give the other conditional: with \(\text{SSR}(\beta) = (\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\beta)^\prime(\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\beta)\)
\[\tau^2 | \mathbf{Y}, \beta \sim \text{Gamma}\bigg(\frac{c_0 + N}{2}, \frac{d_0 + \text{SSR}(\beta)}{2}\bigg)\]

(shape, rate) – the \(\text{Inverse-Gamma}(c_0/2, d_0/2)\) prior on \(\sigma^2\) is a \(\text{Gamma}(c_0/2, d_0/2)\) prior on \(\tau^2\)

So our Gibbs sampler alternates between two easy draws: \(\beta\) from a normal, \(\tau^2\) from a gamma

(Under the conjugate prior \(\beta | \tau^2 \sim \text{Normal}(b_0, (\tau^2 B_0)^{-1})\), the conditional instead has \(V = \big(\tau^2(B_0 + \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})\big)^{-1}\) and \(\mu = (B_0 + \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}(B_0 b_0 + \mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{Y})\))

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Application: Do rejection rates persist?

Last week we saw that the municipalities with the highest 2024 rates still rejected well above the statewide rate in 2022

Is there a systematic relationship between a municipality’s past and present rejection rates?
If clerks differ in how strictly they apply the rules, we’d expect the same places to reject more ballots election after election

Our outcome is a count of rejected ballots

So we’ll fit a binomial logistic regression with the 2022 rejection rate \(x_i\) (in percentage points) as the predictor
We’ll put a normal prior on the \(\beta\) coefficients.

\[Y_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n_i, \pi_i)\] \[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i}\bigg) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\] \[\beta_0, \beta_1 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5^2)\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Plate notation


\(\pi_i\) is now a deterministic quantity: a transformation of \(\beta\) and \(x_i\)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
No conjugate prior

The posterior is (writing \(X_i = (1, x_i)^\prime\), so \(X_i^\prime\beta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\))
\[f(\beta | \mathbf{Y}) \propto \prod_{i=1}^N \bigg[\text{logit}^{-1}(X_i^\prime\beta)^{Y_i}\big(1 - \text{logit}^{-1}(X_i^\prime\beta)\big)^{n_i - Y_i}\bigg] \times \underbrace{\exp\bigg(-\frac{\beta^\prime\beta}{2 \times 5^2}\bigg)}_{\text{Normal}(0, 5^2) \text{ priors}}\]
This isn’t any distribution we recognize, and there’s no prior we could choose to make it workable.

There is no conjugate prior for the logit
(There are data augmentation tricks that give a Gibbs sampler - easier for the probit)

But we can evaluate it for any \(\beta\) - and that’s all we need to implement

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Metropolis-Hastings for the logit

Load the 2022 data and compute each municipality’s 2022 discretionary rejection rate


wi_2022 <- read_csv("data/eavs_2022_wi.csv") %>%
  # 2022 files the Village of Greenville under the old town's code (see data/README.md)
  mutate(FIPSCode = if_else(str_detect(Jurisdiction_Name, "VILLAGE OF GREENVILLE"), "31525", FIPSCode)) %>%
  mutate(n_2022 = C1b - C9b - C9m, y_2022 = C9a - C9b - C9m) %>% filter(n_2022 > 0) %>%
  transmute(FIPSCode, rate_2022 = 100*y_2022/n_2022) # In percentage points
wi <- wi %>% inner_join(wi_2022, by="FIPSCode") # Municipalities with ballots in both years


Set up the regression (1832 municipalities)


X_mat <- model.matrix(~ rate_2022, data=wi)
K <- ncol(X_mat) # Number of beta parameters

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Metropolis-Hastings for the logit

Write a function to evaluate the log of the unnormalized posterior


log_post_logit <- function(b){
  log_lik <- sum(dbinom(wi$y, wi$n, prob = plogis(X_mat %*% b), log=T))
  log_prior <- sum(dnorm(b, mean = 0, sd = 5, log=T))
  log_lik + log_prior
}


Set up the MCMC


M <- 20000  # Number of MCMC samples
burnin <- 5000
beta_mcmc <- matrix(nrow = M, ncol=K) # Matrix to store our samples
beta_mcmc[1,] <- c(0, 0) # Pick a starting value

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Convergence

\(\beta_1\) (the coefficient on the 2022 rate \(x_i\)), including the burn-in period


plot(y=beta_mcmc[,2], x=1:M, xlab="Iteration", ylab="beta_1", type="l")
abline(v=burnin, lty=2, col="indianred")

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Convergence

Both parameters after the burn-in


par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(y=beta_mcmc_use[,1], x=1:nrow(beta_mcmc_use), xlab="Iteration", ylab="beta_0", type="l")
plot(y=beta_mcmc_use[,2], x=1:nrow(beta_mcmc_use), xlab="Iteration", ylab="beta_1", type="l")



\(\beta_1\) bounces around its posterior quickly, but the \(\beta_0\) chain wanders: each draw is highly correlated with the last

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Convergence

Why? Plot the draws of \(\beta_0\) against \(\beta_1\), with both axes on the same scale


data.frame(beta_mcmc_use) %>% ggplot(aes(x=X1, y=X2)) + geom_point(alpha=.05) + coord_fixed() + theme_bw() +
  xlab(expression(beta[0])) + ylab(expression(beta[1]))



The posterior is much wider in \(\beta_0\) (SD 0.031) than in \(\beta_1\) (SD 0.009)
Our proposal takes the same size step (\(\text{SD} = .02\)) in both directions

Large relative to the spread in \(\beta_1\): many proposals land in low-density regions and get rejected
Small relative to the spread in \(\beta_0\): crossing the posterior takes many steps

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Effective sample size

Dependent draws carry less information than independent ones

The effective sample size (ESS) is the number of independent draws that would give an equally precise estimate of the posterior mean



coda::effectiveSize(beta_mcmc_use)

var1 var2 
 539 2398 



We kept 15000 draws, but for \(\beta_0\) they are worth only about 540 independent ones

We could fix this by running much longer, or by tuning the proposal to match the shape of the posterior
Or we could use a smarter algorithm…

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Summaries

Posterior means and 95% credible intervals


beta_mcmc_out <- as.data.frame(beta_mcmc_use)
colnames(beta_mcmc_out) <- c("Intercept", "rate_2022")
data.frame(variable = c("Intercept", "rate_2022"), pm = colMeans(beta_mcmc_out),
           ci95_lower = apply(beta_mcmc_out, 2, function(x) quantile(x, .025)),
           ci95_upper = apply(beta_mcmc_out, 2, function(x) quantile(x, .975)))

           variable     pm ci95_lower ci95_upper
Intercept Intercept -6.254    -6.3135     -6.192
rate_2022 rate_2022  0.116     0.0983      0.132



Compare to the MLE (with 1832 municipalities and a diffuse prior, Bernstein-von Mises says these should be close)


glm(cbind(y, n - y) ~ rate_2022, data = wi, family = binomial) %>% tidy(conf.int = T) %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  term        estimate conf.low conf.high
  <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   -6.25   -6.31      -6.19 
2 rate_2022      0.117   0.0990     0.133

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text: Intro to Stan/HMC

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo improves on the conventional Metropolis-Hastings algorithm by improving the proposals so that they are accepted with very high probability
The method draws on a theoretical core from differential geometry, but it’s not strictly necessary to get the intuition for it.

Betancourt (2017) is a good overview for applied researchers (familiarity with statistics but not physics)

MCMC (ideally) works in 3 general phases

From the starting values, reach the “typical set” of parameter values that occupy most of the posterior mass
The MCMC traverses the “typical set” of values once.
Repeated traversals improve the quality of the MCMC approximation.

Problems arise when Markov Chains

Don’t traverse high density parts of the posterior
Get stuck in parts of the density.

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

Typical distributions for \(Q\) are random walks

In high dimensions, these tend to be bad proposals.

One solution is to choose a low variance for the random walk

This leads to high autocorrelation in the proposals (we just saw this!)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

What if we could come up with a “direction” to point our proposal (or sequence of proposals) that stayed in the “typical set”

Is there another way to get proposals with an acceptance probability of 1 besides Gibbs sampling?

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

Instead of sampling just from \(f(\theta | \mathbf{Y})\), we’ll introduce a set of auxiliary “momentum” variables \(\rho\) and sample from the joint density \(f(\rho, \theta | \mathbf{Y})\).

We’ll generate samples of \(\rho\) and “evolve” \(\theta\) in a particular manner.

That density factors such that if we integrated out the auxiliary variables, we’d get the target.
\[f(\rho, \theta | \mathbf{Y}) = f(\rho | \theta, \mathbf{Y})f(\theta | \mathbf{Y})\]
And we’ll typically pick a distribution on \(\rho\) that is independent of the parameter values.
\[f(\rho, \theta | \mathbf{Y}) = f(\rho)f(\theta | \mathbf{Y})\]
If I propose \(\rho^*\) randomly, how do I find a \(\theta^*\) such that \(f(\rho, \theta | \mathbf{Y}) = f(\rho^*, \theta^* |\mathbf{Y})\) and my acceptance probability is \(1\)?

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

The joint density defines a Hamiltonian \(H(\rho, \theta)\) - in the physics analogy, this is the “total energy” of our system.
\[\begin{align*}H(\rho, \theta) &= -\log f(\rho, \theta | \mathbf{Y})\\
&= - \log f(\rho) - \log f(\theta | \mathbf{Y})\\
&= T(\rho) + V(\theta)\end{align*}\]

\(T(\rho)\) is the “kinetic energy” and \(V(\theta)\) is the “potential energy”

Energy is conserved in this system. So if we randomly choose \(\rho\) and then jointly evolve \(\rho\) and \(\theta\) according to Hamilton’s equations, every point we reach has the same joint density - a proposal that is guaranteed to be accepted.
\[\begin{align*}\frac{d\theta}{dt} &= + \frac{\partial H}{\partial \rho} = \frac{\partial{T}}{\partial{\rho}}\\
\frac{d\rho}{dt} &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta} = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial{\theta}}\end{align*}\]

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

HMC Algorithm (in Stan)

Propose \(\rho^* \sim \text{MultivariateNormal}(0, M)\)
Evolve the joint system of \(\rho^*, \theta^*\) using Hamilton’s equations for some number of steps
Metropolis accept/reject the proposed new set of values (we can only approximate the solution, so the energy isn’t exactly conserved)
Stan’s default, the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), also chooses the number of steps automatically (Hoffman and Gelman 2014)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of HMC

Central intuitions

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is designed to generate proposals with high acceptance probability
These proposals require knowing the gradient of the unnormalized posterior with respect to the parameters

Analytical computation of the gradient is tedious

Numeric computation can be unstable.
Many modern techniques use automatic differentiation

Intuition: Decompose the unnormalized posterior into a series of elementary arithmetic operations and functions where derivatives are trivially known

Use the chain rule to construct the gradient from the component functions + their derivatives.

Downside: Can’t use HMC for discrete parameters (but can often just marginalize those out).

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Overview of Stan

Stan is a C++ library that implements a version of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan Development Team 2024)

Latest iteration of the “model-to-MCMC” libraries like JAGS and BUGS (which are Gibbs samplers)

Key Features

Language agnostic - has interfaces in R, Python, Julia, Stata, etc…
Fast run-time
High-level language for specifying models to be converted to C++ code.

Complications

Running Stan requires you to have the ability to compile C++ code locally
Stan also requires learning a slightly new syntax

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Stan resources

Installation Quick Start Guide
Stan User’s Guide
Stan Reference Manual
Stan Functions Reference
A good model building tutorial for social scientists by Jim Savage

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Installing RStan

We’re working with R, so we’ll be using the rstan interface to Stan
To Install

Install the R-Universe version directly from mc-stan.org/install
There is a nice guide at https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started
Follow the instructions specific to your OS!



# run the next line if you already have rstan installed
# remove.packages(c("StanHeaders", "rstan"))
install.packages("rstan", repos = c('https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev', getOption("repos")))

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Installing RStan

In order to run Stan, your computer needs to be able to compile C++ code. This requires some auxiliary installs that depend on your operating system

Windows: You need to install Rtools. See instructions: RStan wiki: Windows toolchain
Mac: You need the Xcode command line tools and a configured C++ toolchain. The macrtools package sets both up. See instructions: RStan wiki: Mac toolchain
Linux: You need g++ or clang++ - one tends to be installed by default or is available from your repositories.

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Writing a Stan program

Stan programs define a statistical model through a sequence of blocks that identify the data (modeled and unmodeled), parameters, and statistical model.

These are then translated to C++ and compiled. Because Stan uses C++, variables need to be declared differently from a language like R.
C++ is statically typed - the type of a variable needs to be fixed when it is declared.

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Writing a Stan program

Primary variable types and their syntax

int: Integer and real: continuous values
vector and matrix for real-valued column vectors and matrices
array gives an array of any type (like an integer). Stan versions before 2.26 used a different syntax for this.

If variables are constrained, add <lower = .> and <upper = .> to the declaration.
Minor notes

Stan programs in R can be saved as separate files (with a .stan suffix) or in a length 1 character vector (directly typed into R).
Lines end with semi-colons ;
// denotes a comment

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Program blocks

data: Defines the modeled (e.g. \(Y\)) and unmodeled data (e.g. \(X\)) that are used in the model.

Includes any important constants (like the sample size \(N\)) or the number of parameters \(K\) that you don’t hard-code.
When compiling and estimating the model, you’ll pass in R objects for each entry defined in data through a list

Example data block (for our binomial logistic regression):

data {
  int N; // number of municipalities
  int K; // number of covariates
  matrix[N, K] X; // matrix of covariates
  array[N] int<lower=0> n; // number of ballots returned
  array[N] int<lower=0> y; // number of ballots rejected
}

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Program blocks

model: Defines the statistical distributions of the observed data + the parameters

Likelihood and prior distributions

Example model block:

model {
  beta ~ normal(0, 5); // normal prior
  y ~ binomial_logit(n, X * beta); // binomial outcome (logit link)
}

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Program blocks

Other useful (but not required) blocks

functions: Contains user-defined functions that can be used within the remainder of the model definition (or made available to R)
transformed data, transformed parameters: Contains deterministic transformations of either the data or the parameters.
generated quantities: Computes quantities from each posterior draw after estimation (e.g. predictions, simulated data, model summary statistics)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Application: Ballot rejection in Stan

Load the relevant packages


library(rstan)


Pass the data as a list (names must match the data block)


data_source <- list(N = nrow(X_mat), K = ncol(X_mat), X = X_mat, n = wi$n, y = wi$y)

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Application: Ballot rejection in Stan

Run Stan! (The first run takes a minute: Stan has to compile the model to C++)


model_fit <- stan(
  model_code = model_structure,  # Stan code
  data = data_source,     # named list of data
  chains = 4,             # number of Markov chains
  warmup = 500,           # number of warmup iterations per chain
  iter = 2500,            # total number of iterations per chain
  cores = 4,              # number of cores (could use one per chain - by default uses however many you have)
  refresh = 0,            # no progress shown
  seed = 53706
  )


The warmup iterations are like a burn-in, but Stan also uses them to tune the sampler

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Convergence

The traceplot function lets us plot trace plots of any parameters or generated quantities. Let’s do it for \(\beta\)


traceplot(model_fit, pars = c("beta"))



Four chains, started at different random values, all exploring the same region – no wandering

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models
text:
Convergence

Running multiple chains gives us another diagnostic

If every chain has converged to the posterior, they should all look alike
\(\hat{R}\) (“R-hat”) compares the variation between chains to the variation within them
\(\hat{R} \approx 1\) when the chains agree; values above about \(1.01\) are a warning sign

Stan also reports the effective sample size (n_eff) for each parameter

Gives a sense of the Monte Carlo approximation error - this isn’t for statistical inference!

Stan will also warn you about divergent transitions

The simulated trajectory went somewhere the sampler couldn’t follow
Usually a sign of a posterior with a difficult shape!

title: Week 6: Estimating Bayesian Models

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text: “Latent variables” and logit

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Latent variables

Another common way of formulating discrete outcome regressions is in terms of an unobserved continuous “latent” variable and an observation mechanism.

Instead of putting a distribution on \(Y_i\), we put one on an unobserved \(Y_i^*\)
\(Y_i\) is some function of \(Y_i^*\) (usually an indicator function of some sort)

For the logistic regression
\[Y_i = \mathbb{1}(Y_i^* \ge 0)\] \[Y_i^* = X_i^{\prime}\beta + \epsilon_i\] \[\epsilon_i \sim \text{Logistic}(0, 1)\]
The Logistic distribution is parameterized in terms of a “location” (mean) \(\mu\) and a “scale” parameter \(s>0\).

For \(\mu = 0\), \(s= 1\) we have the “standard” logistic

\[\Pr(\epsilon_i \le x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-x)}\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Latent variables

So what’s \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i|X_i] = \Pr(Y_i = 1|X_i)\)?
\[\Pr(Y_i = 1|X_i) = \Pr(Y_i^* \ge 0 | X_i) = \Pr(\epsilon_i \ge -X_i^{\prime}\beta) = \Pr(\epsilon_i \le X_i^{\prime}\beta) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-X_i^{\prime}\beta)}\]

The last-but-one step uses the symmetry of the logistic distribution around zero.

We can write the probit similarly, defining the error distribution as
\[\epsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)\]
And by extension, the probability \(\Pr(Y_i = 1|X_i)\)
\[\Pr(Y_i = 1|X_i) = \Pr(Y_i^* \ge 0|X_i) = \Pr(\epsilon_i \le X_i^{\prime}\beta) = \Phi(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\]
Note the scale of \(\epsilon_i\) is fixed by assumption, not estimated

\(Y_i^*\) is never observed, so only the ratio \(\beta/s\) is identified – so we normalize to \(s =1\)

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Latent variables

We can visualize this as an integral over the density of the random “error” \(\epsilon_i\)

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Latent variables

Same thing for a probit

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Ordinal logit

Using the latent variable formulation lets us extend binary outcome models to outcomes with multiple discrete levels.
For example, consider an “ordinal” response variable

(e.g.) a Likert scale (1 = “strongly disagree”, 3 = “neutral”, 5 = “strongly agree”)

The responses are ordered but the intervals between them do not have any meaning.

A popular modeling technique with an ordinal \(Y\) is to treat it as an expression of a latent variable.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Ordinal logit

In an ordered logit model, an ordinal outcome \(Y\) with \(L\) unique, ordered values \(Y \in \{1, 2, 3, \dotsc L\}\) is a function of a latent variable and a set of \(L-1\) cutpoints \(\kappa\)
\[Y_i = \begin{cases}1 &\text{if } Y_i^* \le \kappa_1 \\
                      2 &\text{if } \kappa_1 < Y_i^* \le \kappa_2\\
                      3 &\text{if } \kappa_2 < Y_i^* \le \kappa_3\\
                      \vdots &\\
                      L &\text{if } Y_i^* > \kappa_{L-1}\end{cases}\]
We still assume \(Y_i^*\) has a logistic distribution
\[Y_i^* = X_i^{\prime}\beta + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \sim \text{Logistic}(0, 1)\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Ordinal logit

To estimate the model, we now have to estimate both the \(\beta\) parameters and the \(\kappa\) parameters

Note we omit the intercept from \(X_i\) – the \(\kappa\) parameters are essentially the “intercepts” for each boundary between the choices.

How does the model map changes in the latent variable to changes in probability? Work with the cumulative probabilities:
\[\Pr(Y_i \le l \,|\, X_i) = \Pr(Y_i^* \le \kappa_l \,|\, X_i) = \Pr(\epsilon_i \le \kappa_l - X_i^{\prime}\beta)\]
And then difference adjacent cumulatives to get each cell probability
\[\Pr(Y_i = l \,|\, X_i) = \Pr(Y_i \le l \,|\, X_i) - \Pr(Y_i \le l-1 \,|\, X_i)\]
with the conventions \(\Pr(Y_i \le 0) = 0\) and \(\Pr(Y_i \le L) = 1\).

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Ordinal logit

Let’s think in terms of the distribution of \(Y_i^*\) and the cut-points for a case with \(L=3\). For \(X_i^{\prime}\beta = 0\):



The green lines are the cutpoints \(\kappa_1, \kappa_2\); the shaded areas are \(\Pr(Y_i = 1), \Pr(Y_i = 2), \Pr(Y_i = 3)\).

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Ordinal logit

Shifting the mean of \(Y^*\) up by 3:



The cutpoints stay put but the distribution slides. All three probabilities move together as a result.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Ordinal logit

This structural mapping from \(Y^*\) to \(\Pr(Y_i = l)\) encodes a particular assumption about how these probabilities relate to one another.
Referred to as the proportional odds assumption
\[\log\left(\frac{\Pr(Y_i \le l)}{1 - \Pr(Y_i \le l)}\right) = \kappa_l - X_i^{\prime}\beta\]

The same \(\beta\) appears for every \(l\); only the intercept \(\kappa_l\) changes.

Intuitively: the \(\beta\) parameters are shared across all the possible outcome levels.

Information about whether someone responds “strongly agree” also tells us something about how likely they would be to respond “agree”, “neutral”, “disagree”, or “strongly disagree”.
Not innocuous if there’s non-monotonicity or heterogeneous effects.
Be careful with these models!

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Multinomial logit

In a setting with multiple unordered outcomes, the natural extension of the logit regression is the multinomial logit
Suppose we have an outcome with \(K\) unordered levels (e.g. “choices”). Define a latent “utility” \(Y_{ik}^*\) for each of the \(K\) categories

For identification, we set one category to be the “baseline” by anchoring its coefficients to zero: \(\beta_1 = 0\)

\[\begin{align*}Y_{i1}^* &= X_i^{\prime}\beta_1 + \epsilon_{i1} = \epsilon_{i1}\\
Y_{i2}^* &= X_i^{\prime}\beta_2 + \epsilon_{i2}\\
&\vdots \\
Y_{iK}^* &= X_i^{\prime}\beta_K + \epsilon_{iK}\end{align*}\]
The probability of observing choice \(Y_{i} = k\) is the probability that the \(k\)th latent variable is greater than all of the others
\[\Pr(Y_i = k \,|\, X_i) = \Pr\big(Y^*_{ik} = \max\{Y^*_{i1}, Y^*_{i2}, \dotsc Y^*_{iK}\}\big)\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Multinomial logit

It turns out that if the error terms \(\epsilon_{ik}\) have i.i.d. “Type I extreme value” distributions, we can write the choice probabilities in closed form
\[\Pr(Y_i = k \,|\, X_i) = \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta_{k})}{\sum_{k^\prime=1}^K \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta_{k^\prime})}\]
This is sometimes referred to as the “softmax” function in machine learning.
Note: with the normalized baseline category \(\beta_1 = 0\), we can write this equivalently as
\[\Pr(Y_i = k \,|\, X_i) = \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta_{k})}{1 + \sum_{k^\prime=2}^K \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta_{k^\prime})}\]
The i.i.d. error assumption implies independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA).

The relative odds of choice \(k\) vs. \(l\) don’t depend on what other options are available.
Famously implausible in some choice settings (the “red bus/blue bus” problem).

Example: Appointer Affiliation Bias

Puig and Strezhnev (2017) ran a survey experiment on a group of international arbitration experts to see how manipulating the appointing party affected their decisionmaking in a vignette

Respondents were given a hypothetical dispute and asked to determine who should pay the legal costs
Three options: Loser pays all, Loser pays some, Both sides split

Remember, don’t just fixate on the outcome when choosing a modeling strategy - think about what your entire bundle of assumptions implies!

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Conditional logit

Same latent utility setup as the multinomial logit, but now the covariates are attribute-specific but their types are shared across alternatives

Price of each mode of transportation, the attributes of each profile in a conjoint

\(X_{ik}\) varies across categories, but all categories share a common \(\beta\) vector
\[Y_{ik}^* = X_{ik}^{\prime}\beta + \epsilon_{ik}\]
With the same i.i.d. Type I extreme value errors, we get the same “softmax” expression for the choice probability.
\[\Pr(Y_i = k \,|\, X_{i1}, \dotsc, X_{iK}) = \frac{\exp(X_{ik}^{\prime}\beta)}{\sum_{k^\prime=1}^K \exp(X_{ik^\prime}^{\prime}\beta)}\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
IIA

We still have the independence of irrelevant alternatives assumption: the relative odds of two choices only depend on those two choices’ attributes.
\[\frac{\Pr(Y_i = j)}{\Pr(Y_i = k)} = \exp\big((X_{ij} - X_{ik})^{\prime}\beta\big)\]
Extensions involve imposing additional hierarchical structure:

Nested logit - group similar alternatives and allow correlation within groupings

A random effect common to every alternative in the same group \(g(k)\): \(Y_{ik}^* = X_{ik}^{\prime}\beta + \zeta_{i,g(k)} + \epsilon_{ik}\)

Mixed logit / random coefficients – let \(\beta\) vary across individuals (Train 2009)

Unit-specific coefficients drawn from a common distribution: \(Y_{ik}^* = X_{ik}^{\prime}\beta_i + \epsilon_{ik}\)

Increasingly estimated via Bayesian methods (for regularization + partial pooling)

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Conjoint experiments

A conjoint experiment shows respondents two (or more) profiles with randomly assigned attributes and asks them to pick one.

e.g. choosing between two candidates with different backgrounds, partisan affiliation, policy positions, etc…

Often designed as a forced choice between alternatives described by alternative-specific covariates
In political science: analyzed as a factorial experiment

Estimand is the AMCE (Hainmueller et al. 2014) – the average change in the probability of selection from changing one attribute, marginalizing over the others.
Estimated by OLS, no distributional assumptions, “causal” interpretation.

In literally every other field that does conjoints: analyzed with a random utility model

Model latent utilities and simulate choice probabilities.

Plus pay and benefits, hours, location, owners’ race and gender, unionization, political donations, workplace conditions, …

The paper reports AMCEs from OLS. We’ll fit the conditional logit to the same choices.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text: Survival models

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Survival models

Often we have outcome data that is measured as the “time-to-event”

From the medical literature, this is often the number of days before a patient suffers some adverse event (e.g. death).
But lots of other applications (e.g. time to treaty ratification)

Assume we observe \(n\) i.i.d. event times \(T_1, T_2, \dotsc, T_n\)
Define the “survival function”
\[S(t) = Pr(T > t) = 1 - F(t)\]
We’ll also often work with the “hazard” or the “instantaneous” probability of an event happening given that it has not yet occurred
\[h(t) = \underset{\Delta t \to 0}{\lim} \frac{P(t < T_i \le t + \Delta t | T_i > t)}{\Delta t} = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)} = \frac{f(t)}{1-F(t)}\]
Intuitively: Given that I know that an event has not occurred until \(t\), what is the probability that it will immediately occur next!

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Survival models

We’ll also define the cumulative hazard
\[H(t) = \int_{0}^{t} h(u)du = \int_0^{t} \frac{f(u)}{S(u)} du =  -\log(S(t))\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Non-parametric approach

The easiest way to estimate \(S(t) = 1 - F(t)\) is to just plug in \(\hat{F}(t)\) - our empirical CDF in the sample

At any given value \(t\), what share of events occur after \(t\)

Problem: This doesn’t address censoring of observations – sometimes we stop observing a unit at time \(t^*\) rather than observing an actual event.

We know that \(T_i > t^*\) but not what \(T_i\) actually equals

Let \(C = \{C_1, C_2, \dotsc, C_n\}\) denote the censoring indicator

If \(C_i = 1\), then the observation is censored, the observed value \(t\) only gives us information on \(T_i > t\) as opposed to \(T_i = t\).
Crucially, we assume that censoring is “uninformative”

One approach to constructing a non-parametric estimator of the survival function under censoring is the Kaplan-Meier estimator.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Kaplan-Meier Estimator

Start by arranging the possible event times from \(0 < t_{(1)} < t_{(2)} < t_{(3)} < t_{(4)}, \dotsc, < t_{(n)}\)

Suppose \(t\) is after \(t_{(j)}\) and before \(t_{(j+1)}\). We can write the survival function in terms of conditional probabilities:

\[S(t) = Pr(T_i > t | T_i > t_{(j)}) \times Pr(T_i > t_{(j)} | T_i > t_{(j-1)}) \times \dotsc \times Pr(T_i > t_{(2)} | T_i  > t_{(1)}) \times Pr(T_i > t_{(1)})\]
The Kaplan-Meier estimator \(\hat{S}(t)\) is a “plug-in” estimator for each of these probabilities.
\[\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{j: t_{(j)} \le t} \bigg(1 - \frac{d_j}{r_j} \bigg)\]
\(d_j\) denotes the number of units that experience an event at time \(t_{(j)}\)
\(r_j\) is the number of units that are still in the risk set just before \(t_{(j)}\)

Units drop out of the risk set \(r\) over time by either experiencing an event or being censored

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Kaplan-Meier Estimator

Intuition: Consider one of the terms in the product. Using the definition of conditional probability:
\[Pr(T_i > t_{(j)} | T_i > t_{(j-1)}) = 1 - Pr(T_i \le t_{(j)}|T_i > t_{(j-1)}) = 1 - \frac{Pr(T_i \le t_{(j)}, T_i > t_{(j-1)})}{Pr(T_i > t_{(j-1)})}\]
In the numerator, our “plug-in” estimator is just the share of units that have events occurring at \(t_{(j)}\).
In the denominator we have the share of units that we know for sure are still “active” in the interval after \(t_{(j-1)}\)
Hence our overall “plug-in” estimator:
\[\widehat{Pr}(T_i > t_{(j)} | T_i > t_{(j-1)}) = 1 - \frac{d_j}{r_j}\]
Taking the product across all of the \(j\) where \(t_{(j)} \le t\) yields the Kaplan-Meier estimator.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Parametric inference

When we want to model the survival function using covariates, we run into a clear constraint using purely non-parametric methods

Splitting the sample and constructing separate K-M curves for each unique covariate profile quickly becomes infeasible.

We may want to assume a model for the event time. We can write that density in terms of the hazard and the survival function
\[f(t) = h(t)S(t)\]
Note that by the definition of the cumulative hazard \(H(t) = - \log(S(t))\) and \(S(t) = \exp(-H(t))\), so
\[f(t) = h(t)\exp(-H(t))\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Parametric inference

Depending on the assumptions we make about the nature of the hazard, we can obtain different distributions for \(f(t)\).

In the simplest case, let’s assume that the hazard does not vary over time: \(h(t) = \lambda\), with \(\lambda > 0\)
And the cumulative hazard is \(H(t) = \int_{0}^{t} \lambda du = \lambda t\)

This yields the exponential distribution
\[f(t) = \lambda \exp(-\lambda t)\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Exponential Model

The mean of \(T_i \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\) is \(E[T_i] = \frac{1}{\lambda}\). We’ll often reparameterize the mean as \(\theta\), yielding a density of
\[f(t) = \frac{1}{\theta} \exp\bigg(-\frac{1}{\theta} t\bigg)\]
\(\theta\) is strictly greater than \(0\), so we’ll use a log-link to incorporate the covariates:
\[\log(E[T_i | X_i]) = \log(\theta_i) = X_i^{\prime}\beta\]
Alternatively, we can write
\[E[T_i | X_i] = \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\]
Note that the constant hazard assumption is strong

The exponential distribution is “memoryless” in that knowing that a unit has survived up until time \(t\) tells you nothing about its instantaneous probability of failure.
More flexible distributions like the Weibull allow for a time-varying hazard.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Exponential Model

We can interpret changes in the linear predictor in terms of changes in the hazard since

\[h(t) = \frac{1}{\theta_i} = \frac{1}{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}\]

Increases in the linear predictor reduce the hazard.
This also lets us write down the survival function

\[S(t) = \exp\bigg(- \frac{1}{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}t \bigg)\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Application

Let’s compare our parametric fit to the non-parametric Kaplan-Meier estimates


# sex = 2 is a dummy variable for female
exp_model_sex <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ I(sex==2), dist="exponential", data=lung)


Get the survival curves for men and women


exp_surv_men <- function(x) pexp(x, rate = 1/exp(coef(exp_model_sex)%*%c(1,0)), lower.tail = F)
exp_surv_women <- function(x) pexp(x, rate = 1/exp(coef(exp_model_sex)%*%c(1,1)), lower.tail=F)

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Application

Overlay the exponential survival curves on the Kaplan-Meier estimates

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Application: Weibull

The fit seems to be off.

This is because the hazard appears to be time-varying.
You can see a kind of “s-curve” which the exponential cannot capture.

The Weibull adds a shape parameter \(k\) that lets the hazard change over time
\[h(t) = \frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{t}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}\qquad S(t) = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{t}{\lambda}\right)^{k}\right)\]

\(k = 1\) is the exponential; \(k > 1\) is a rising hazard, \(k < 1\) a falling one



weib_model_sex <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ I(sex==2), dist="weibull", data=lung)

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Application: Weibull

Get the Weibull survival curves (\(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\)) and overlay them on Kaplan-Meier


weib_surv_men <- function(x) pweibull(x, shape = 1/weib_model_sex$scale,
                                       scale = exp(coef(weib_model_sex)%*%c(1,0)), lower.tail = F)
weib_surv_women <- function(x) pweibull(x, shape = 1/weib_model_sex$scale,
                                         scale = exp(coef(weib_model_sex)%*%c(1,1)), lower.tail = F)

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Cox Proportional Hazards

The Cox proportional hazards model assumes that covariates enter the hazard log-linearly, but the baseline hazard is unspecified

\[h_i(t) =  h_0(t)\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\]

\(h_0(t)\) is the unknown baseline hazard function.
Note that while the baseline hazard is not explicitly identified, the ratio of the hazards of two observations \(i\) and \(j\) at time \(t\) does not depend on the baseline
\[\frac{h_i(t)}{h_j(t)} = \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}{\exp(X_j^{\prime}\beta)}\]
The model is semi-parametric in that some components are left entirely unspecified…

…but others are not – we assume that the covariates act proportionally on the hazard irrespective of time.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Cox Proportional Hazards

The model is estimated by maximizing a partial likelihood

We observe event time \(Y_i\) - assume no ties

The individual partial likelihood is
\[L_i(\beta) = \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}{\sum_{k; Y_k \ge Y_i} \exp(X_k^{\prime}\beta)}\]
Intuitively: The denominator contains the hazards of all observations in the risk set at the event time \(Y_i\)
Then the full likelihood is just the product over all the individual partial likelihoods
\[L(\beta) = \prod_{i: C_i = 0}  \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}{\sum_{k; Y_k \ge Y_i} \exp(X_k^{\prime}\beta)}\]

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Cox and conditional logit

The individual partial likelihood should look familiar - it has exactly the form of the conditional logit
\[L_i(\beta) = \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}{\sum_{k; Y_k \ge Y_i} \exp(X_k^{\prime}\beta)}\]
At each event time we are asking: given that one unit in the risk set failed, which one was it?

The “choice set” is the risk set \(\{k: Y_k \ge Y_i\}\), and the “chosen alternative” is the unit that failed.

title: Week 4: More Likelihood Models
text:
Application

What does the Cox fit look like


# sex = 2 is a dummy variable for female
cox_model_sex <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ I(sex==2), data=lung)
print(cox_model_sex)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ I(sex == 2), data = lung)

                coef exp(coef) se(coef)  z     p
I(sex == 2)TRUE -0.5       0.6      0.2 -3 0.001

Likelihood ratio test=11  on 1 df, p=0.001
n= 228, number of events= 165 



Note that we don’t get an estimate of the hazard because the baseline is left unspecified

If we want to plot survival curves, we’ll need some estimate of \(h_0\) using another method (like Kaplan-Meier)

text:

Estimate the baseline cumulative hazard non-parametrically (the Breslow estimator) and get the Cox-predicted survival curves for men and women


cox_surv_sex <- survfit(cox_model_sex, newdata = data.frame(sex = c(1, 2)))

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Previously

Likelihood: a function of the parameters \(\theta\) evaluated at the observed data
\[\mathcal{L}(\theta| \mathbf{y}) = f(\mathbf{y}| \theta) \qquad \ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(y_i|\theta)\]
Maximum likelihood estimator: \(\hat{\theta} = \argmax_{\theta \in \Theta} \ \ell_n(\theta)\)

Consistent: \(\hat{\theta} \overset{p}{\to} \theta_0\)
Asymptotically normal: \(\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta} - \theta_0) \overset{d}{\to} \text{Normal}\big(0, \mathcal{I}(\theta_0)^{-1}\big)\)
Asymptotically efficient: attains the Cramér-Rao lower bound

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
This week

More properties of the MLE

Invariance and the delta method

How does numerical optimization actually work?

Newton-Raphson, Fisher scoring, gradient ascent

Generalized linear models

Extending the classic linear form to functions of the CEF
\(g(\mathbb{E}[Y_i|X_i]) = X_i^{\prime}\beta\)

Binary outcome models

Logit and probit; deriving and estimating the likelihood
Interpretation: log-odds, marginal effects, and the delta method

An application: propensity scores and inverse probability weighting

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text: More on the MLE

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Invariance

We often want to do inference on some function of \(\theta\)

(e.g.) we estimate \(\beta\) but want a predicted probability, a risk ratio, or a marginal effect.

The MLE has a convenient property: invariance.

If \(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat{\theta})\) is the MLE of \(g(\theta)\) – for any function \(g\).

Combined with consistency, \(g(\hat{\theta}) \overset{p}{\to} g(\theta_0)\) for continuous \(g\) (continuous mapping theorem).
But how do we get the standard errors (asymptotically)?

The delta method

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Delta method

We know the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\theta}\)

It’s the inverse Fisher information, estimated by the inverse negative Hessian at the MLE.

To get \(\text{Var}(g(\hat{\theta}))\), start with a first-order Taylor approximation around the true value \(\theta_0\)
\[g(\hat{\theta}) \approx g(\theta_0) + \big[\nabla g(\theta_0)^{\prime}\big](\hat{\theta} - \theta_0)\]
Take the variance
\[\text{Var}\big(g(\hat{\theta})\big) \approx \text{Var}\bigg(g(\theta_0) + \big[\nabla g(\theta_0)^{\prime}\big]\hat{\theta} - \big[\nabla g(\theta_0)^{\prime}\big]\theta_0\bigg)\]
\(g(\theta_0)\) and \(\nabla g(\theta_0)\) are constants, so the variance of the first and third terms is zero
\[\text{Var}\big(g(\hat{\theta})\big) \approx \text{Var}\bigg(\big[\nabla g(\theta_0)^{\prime}\big]\hat{\theta}\bigg)\]

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Delta method

Pull out and “square” the constant. We get an expression in terms of the original variance-covariance matrix
\[\text{Var}\big(g(\hat{\theta})\big) \approx \big[\nabla g(\theta_0)^{\prime}\big]\text{Var}(\hat{\theta})\big[\nabla g(\theta_0)\big]\]
And so our asymptotic approximation is
\[\sqrt{n}\big(g(\hat{\theta}) - g(\theta_0)\big) \overset{d}{\to} \text{Normal}\bigg(0, \ \big[\nabla g(\theta_0)^{\prime}\big]\mathcal{I}(\theta_0)^{-1}\big[\nabla g(\theta_0)\big]\bigg)\]
We can use a plug-in estimator at the MLE: evaluate the gradient at \(\hat{\theta}\) and use our existing estimator \(\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\theta})\).

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text: How optimizers work

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Finding the maximum

How does maxLik() actually find a solution?
Our estimator is defined as
\[\hat{\theta} = \argmax_{\theta \in \Theta} \ \ell_n(\theta)\]
For well-behaved problems the log-likelihood is concave, so finding the maximum amounts to finding the unique solution to \(S_n(\theta) = 0\).
Closed form solutions are rare (the Normal linear model is a special case).

Generally, we’ll use an iterative algorithm to find this solution.

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Newton-Raphson

We start at some initial guess \(\hat{\theta}^{(0)}\)
Let \(\hat{\theta}^{(t)}\) denote the “current” value and \(\hat{\theta}^{(t+1)}\) our update – we keep iterating until convergence.
Our goal is to solve for a zero of \(S_n(\theta)\). Take a first-order Taylor approximation around our current guess
\[S_n(\theta) \approx S_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)}) + \nabla S_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)}) \left(\theta - \hat{\theta}^{(t)}\right)\]
What’s \(\nabla S_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)})\)?

It’s the Jacobian of the gradient… or the matrix of second-order partial derivatives of the log-likelihood… or the Hessian \(H_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)})\)!

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Newton-Raphson

Our next value of \(\hat{\theta}\) is the value that sets this approximation to zero
\[0 =  S_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)}) + H_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)}) \left(\hat{\theta}^{(t+1)} - \hat{\theta}^{(t)}\right)\]
Multiply through by the inverse Hessian and rearrange
\[\hat{\theta}^{(t+1)} =  \hat{\theta}^{(t)} - H_n^{-1}(\hat{\theta}^{(t)}) S_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)})\]
Recall that the negative Hessian at \(\hat\theta\) is the observed Fisher information \(\mathcal{J}_n(\hat\theta) = -H_n(\hat\theta)\)

So the update is the score scaled by the inverse negative hessian.

An alternative algorithm, Fisher scoring, substitutes the expected Fisher information \(\mathcal{I}_n\) for the observed one.

Identical for GLMs with the canonical link – we’ll see why later.

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Gradient ascent

Compare the Newton-Raphson update to the classic “gradient descent/gradient ascent” algorithm
\[\hat{\theta}^{(t+1)} =  \hat{\theta}^{(t)} + \gamma_t S_n(\hat{\theta}^{(t)})\]
Gradient ascent chooses some sequence of \(\gamma_t\) (the “learning rate” or “step size”) at iteration \(t\)

The gradient tells us which direction to move in and \(\gamma_t\) tells us how far to move.

Contrast with Newton-Raphson, where “how far to move” comes from computing and inverting the Hessian

More information per step, but each step is computationally expensive (inverting a matrix is computationally hard)

Trade-off: Newton-Raphson converges quickly but each step is costly; gradient ascent steps are cheap but need more of them.

Also typically need to tune the learning rate \(\gamma_t\) - too large and we overshoot the true optimum

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Illustration

Let’s illustrate with a simple one-parameter likelihood.
\[y_i \underset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(\pi), \qquad \pi = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\theta)}\]

One parameter \(\theta\), the log-odds of success.

The average log-likelihood, its score, and its Hessian all have closed forms
\[\bar{\ell}_n(\theta) = \bar{y}\,\theta - \log\big(1 + e^{\theta}\big), \qquad \bar{S}_n(\theta) = \bar{y} - \pi, \qquad \bar{H}_n(\theta) = -\pi(1-\pi)\]
The Newton-Raphson step can be written in closed form
\[\hat{\theta}^{(t+1)} = \hat{\theta}^{(t)} + \frac{\bar{y} - \pi^{(t)}}{\pi^{(t)}\big(1 - \pi^{(t)}\big)}\]
And the true MLE is also known in closed form: \(\hat{\theta} = \log\frac{\bar{y}}{1-\bar{y}}\)

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Coding the two algorithms

Simulate some data and write down the three components


set.seed(60637)
n <- 100
y <- rbinom(n, 1, 1/(1 + exp(-0.8)))   # true theta = 0.8
ybar <- mean(y)

loglik <- function(th) ybar*th - log(1 + exp(th))      # average log-likelihood
score  <- function(th) ybar - 1/(1 + exp(-th))         # average score
hess   <- function(th){ p <- 1/(1 + exp(-th)); -p*(1-p) }  # average Hessian

theta_hat <- log(ybar/(1 - ybar))                      # the analytic MLE
theta_hat

[1] 0.895

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Coding the two algorithms

Start both at \(\hat{\theta}^{(0)} = -1\)


nr_path <- newton(-1, iter = 4)
ga_path <- grad_ascent(-1, gamma = 1, iter = 12)
round(nr_path, 6)

[1] -1.000  1.243  0.863  0.895  0.895



round(ga_path, 6)

 [1] -1.0000 -0.5589 -0.2127  0.0503  0.2477  0.3961  0.5083  0.5939  0.6597
[10]  0.7105  0.7500  0.7808  0.8049

Gradient ascent has taken twelve steps and still isn’t there.

text: Intro to GLMs

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Motivation: Propensity Scores

Researchers wanting to estimate causal effects from observational designs often use a weighting estimator to account for non-random treatment assignment.

Observe treatment \(D_i\), confounders \(X_i\), outcome \(Y_i\)
Need to estimate the propensity score \(\pi_i = \Pr(D_i = 1 | X_i)\) to construct “inverse propensity of treatment weights”

Key problem: with many continuous covariates, it’s hard to estimate \(\Pr(D_i = 1 | X_i)\) non-parametrically

One solution: assume a parametric model for \(D_i\).

Propensity scores are predictions from the model.

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
The LaLonde dataset

LaLonde (1986) asked: can selection-on-observables designs recover the answer from a randomized experiment?

The National Supported Work Demonstration (NSW) randomly assigned disadvantaged workers to a job training program.
Outcome: real earnings in 1978 (re78).
Because assignment was random, the experiment gives a credible benchmark: roughly $1,794 for the subsample we’ll use (Dehejia and Wahba 1999).

LaLonde created an observational dataset by replacing the experimental controls with a survey comparison group drawn from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID).

Now treatment is not randomly assigned – the comparison group is much older, better educated, and far richer at baseline.
If our adjustment methods work, they should recover something near $1,794 anyway.

LaLonde (1986) found typical OLS regression worked poorly

Dehejia and Wahba (1999) tackle this with propensity score methods (specifically matching, but we’ll do weighting).

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
The experimental benchmark

The experimental controls are not in that dataset – LaLonde replaced them. But they ship alongside it.


data(lalonde.exp)   # 185 treated + 260 *randomized* controls
lalonde.exp %>% group_by(treat) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), age = mean(age), education = mean(education),
            married = mean(married), re74 = mean(re74))

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  treat     n   age education married  re74

1     0   260  25.1      10.1   0.154 2107.
2     1   185  25.8      10.3   0.189 2096.



Randomization did its job – the two arms look alike on every pre-treatment covariate.


exp_att <- lm_robust(re78 ~ treat, data = lalonde.exp, se_type = "HC2")
coef(summary(exp_att))["treat",]

The 185 treated units are the same people in both datasets; only the comparison group changes.
Note the benchmark is itself an estimate, with a 95% CI of roughly \([\$476,\ \$3{,}113]\).

The naive comparison

Regressing 1978 earnings on treatment alone:

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Generalized Linear Models

Generalized linear models (GLMs) (Nelder and Wedderburn 1972) have three components:

A parametric distribution for \(Y_i|X_i\) (“stochastic component”)
A linear predictor: \(\eta_i = X_i^{\prime}\beta = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \beta_2X_{i2} + \dotsc + \beta_kX_{ik}\) (“systematic component”)
A link function \(g()\) applied to the CEF \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i|X_i]\) that yields the linear predictor
\[g\big(\mathbb{E}[Y_i | X_i]\big) = \eta_i\]

Alternatively, we can write the CEF in terms of the “inverse link” \(g^{-1}()\) applied to the linear predictor
$$\mathbb{E}[Y_i | X_i] = g^{-1}(\eta_i)$$

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Exponential Family

The types of probability distributions permitted for \(Y_i\) are quite general: the exponential family

This contains the Normal as well as many other common distributions – the Bernoulli, Poisson, exponential, gamma, and more.

Exponential family distributions have density functions of the form
\[f(Y|\theta) = h(Y) \exp\bigg\{b(\theta) \cdot T(Y) - A(\theta)\bigg\}\]
\(h(Y)\), \(b(\theta)\), \(T(Y)\) and \(A(\theta)\) are known functions

\(T(Y)\) is the sufficient statistic, \(b(\theta)\) the canonical (natural) parameter, \(A(\theta)\) the log-normalizer.

The key intuition: exponential family distributions factorize in a convenient way

The parameter and the data interact only through the product \(b(\theta) \cdot T(Y)\).
If \(b(\theta) = \theta\), the distribution is in “canonical” form.

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Example: Bernoulli

Consider the Bernoulli PMF
\[f(Y_i|\pi_i) = \pi_i^{Y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-Y_i}\]
Take the log, then the exponent
\[f(Y_i|\pi_i) = \exp\bigg\{\log\bigg[\pi_i^{Y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-Y_i}\bigg]\bigg\}\]
Properties of logs
\[f(Y_i|\pi_i) = \exp\bigg\{Y_i\log(\pi_i) + (1-Y_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\bigg\}\]

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Example: Bernoulli

Rearranging and using properties of logs again
\[f(Y_i|\pi_i) = \exp\bigg\{Y_i\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg) + \log(1-\pi_i)\bigg\}\]
So our exponential form is

\(h(Y) = 1\)
\(T(Y) = Y_i\)
\(b(\pi_i) = \log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg)\)
\(A(\pi_i) = -\log(1-\pi_i)\)

remember the exponential form carries a minus sign in front of \(A\)


Critically, this is where we get a good link function

The canonical parameter is \(\log\bigg(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\bigg)\) – the log-odds.
The canonical link is the function that equates this parameter with the linear predictor: \(\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg) = X_i^{\prime}\beta\)

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text: Binary outcome models

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Logistic regression

The “logit” or “logistic” GLM models the log-odds of a binary outcome as a function of the linear predictor \(X_i^{\prime}\beta\)
\[Y_i \underset{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)\]
\[\mathbb{E}[Y_i | X_i] = \Pr(Y_i = 1 | X_i) = \pi_i\]
\[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg) = X_i^{\prime}\beta\]
Alternatively, this is written in terms of the “inverse link” function (the logistic function) relating \(\pi_i\) to \(g^{-1}(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\)
\[\pi_i = \frac{\exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}{1 + \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-X_i^{\prime}\beta)}\]

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Inverse-link functions

The logistic function maps inputs on \(\mathbb{R}\) to \((0, 1)\)

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Inverse-link functions

Another link is the “probit”, whose inverse link is the Normal CDF \(\Phi()\)

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Inverse-link functions

When do we use probit vs. logit?

Computational convenience – the logit is the canonical link, so it’s better behaved.
Probit has some good properties for Bayesian inference (we’ll come back to this).

Can you tell the difference?

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Deriving the logit likelihood

Start from the Bernoulli log-likelihood
\[\ell_n(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\log(\pi_i) + (1-Y_i)\log(1 - \pi_i)\]
Collecting the \(Y_i\) terms gives us the log-odds, which is just \(X_i^{\prime}\beta\)
\[\ell_n(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i \log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg) + \log(1 - \pi_i)\]
And from the inverse link,
\[1 - \pi_i = 1 -  \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-X_i^{\prime}\beta)} = \frac{\exp(-X_i^{\prime}\beta)}{1 + \exp(-X_i^{\prime}\beta)} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)}\]
Substituting in
\[\ell_n(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \bigg[Y_i X_i^{\prime}\beta - \log\bigg(1 + \exp(X_i^{\prime}\beta)\bigg)\bigg]\]

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Interpreting logit coefficients

How do we interpret the \(\beta\) parameters substantively?
\[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \beta_2X_{i2} + \dotsc + \beta_k X_{ik}\]
Take the partial derivative w.r.t. \(X_{ik}\)
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial X_{ik}} \log\bigg(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\bigg) =  \beta_k\]
So \(\beta_k\) captures the change in the log-odds for a one-unit change in \(X_{k}\)

Descriptively, it’s the difference in log-odds between two observations that differ in \(X_{k}\) by one unit.
Exponentiating, \(\exp(\beta_k)\) is an odds ratio. This is not a risk ratio, and it is not a difference in probabilities.

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Interpreting logit coefficients

On the “log-odds” scale, the change due to an increase in \(X_{k}\) does not depend on the values of the other \(X\) variables (unless we explicitly specify an interaction).

But thinking on the log-odds scale is hard! We think in terms of probabilities.
This additivity does not hold when we take \(\frac{\partial}{\partial X_{i1}} \pi_i\)

Working through the chain rule,
\[\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial X_{ik}} = \beta_k \, \pi_i(1 - \pi_i)\]

The effect on the probability scale depends on \(\pi_i\), and therefore on every covariate.

Logit models implicitly encode interactions with respect to the CEF \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i | X_i]\).

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Interpreting logit coefficients

Remember: A one-unit change in the linear predictor corresponds to different changes in probability depending on your baseline.

title: Week 3: Generalized Linear Models
text:
Transformed quantities

We have \(\hat{\beta}\), but we actually want the propensity score \(\hat{\pi}_i = \Pr(D_i = 1 | X_i)\)

Just apply the inverse link to get the quantity we want

\[\hat{\pi}_i = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-X_i^{\prime}\hat{\beta})}\]
By invariance, this is the MLE of \(\pi_i\), and it’s consistent for the true propensity score (under our modeling assumptions).
But if we want a confidence interval for \(\hat{\pi}_i\), we use the delta method.

marginaleffects

The marginaleffects R package provides a straightforward implementation of the delta method for a lot of transformed quantities

(e.g.) the marginal change in the probability of \(D_i=1\) for a one-unit change in \(X\)

avg_predictions() will calculate point estimates + CIs for the expected outcome just like we did above.
avg_comparisons() will do the implied “marginal effects” for a unit change in \(X\) given a set baseline.
We have to tell it which covariate profile to evaluate at. We’ll use the treated units – the NSW participants are the group we care about.
