title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Hierarchical Models

In our regression models so far, we assumed a common intercept and slope for all of the data.

The underlying model is the same regardless of which group (e.g. state) an observation is located in.

We also assumed that observations were completely exchangeable

\(Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(X_i^{\prime}\beta, \sigma^2)\) implies no residual correlation in the outcomes across all observations.

This may be a poor modeling choice if states are very heterogeneous and information about the state in which an observation is located would provide additional predictive power beyond knowing \(X_i\).

Additionally, exchangeability of observations may be violated - unobserved factors may lead observations within a particular state to be correlated (e.g. if all respondents in a state are exposed to some common shock).

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Hierarchical Models

Hierarchical or Multilevel linear models try to address this by incorporating additional structure on the regression parameters.

Suppose observations belong to a group \(j \in \{1, 2, 3, \dotsc, J\}\) (e.g. states, time periods, schools, etc…)
We observe \(Y_{ij}\) as the outcome for unit \(i\) in grouping \(j\).

We can incorporate group membership into the data-generating process.
Instead of a common prior on \(\beta \sim \text{Normal}(b_0, B_0^{-1})\), we may do something like:
\[\beta_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{\beta}, \Sigma_{\beta})\]
\[Y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(X_{ij}^{\prime}\beta_{j}, \sigma^2)\]
This model assumes that each group has its own set of group-level coefficients \(\beta_j\) that are drawn from a common distribution centered at \(\mu_{\beta}\).
The variance \(\Sigma_{\beta}\) then dictates the degree of pooling across groupings.

Infinite variance (a flat prior on each \(\beta_j\)): no pooling - \(\beta_j\) are estimated entirely separately
Zero variance: complete pooling (all \(\beta_j\) are equal to \(\mu_{\beta}\))
In between: partial pooling - and we can estimate \(\mu_{\beta}\) and \(\Sigma_{\beta}\) from the data

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Hierarchical Models

There are lots of choices about how we want to incorporate hierarchy into the model the coefficients across groupings

What levels of aggregation and how many?
Which parameters should be allowed to vary (all of the coefficients or just the intercepts)?
Where does the structure enter into the model (the means? the variances? the covariances?)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Application: Education polarization

A growing divide in American politics centers on education

Voters with a college degree have moved towards the Democrats over the last decade
Voters without one have moved towards the Republicans

Is the education gap the same everywhere?

Gelman et al. (2007) found that the relationship between income and vote choice differs across states: steep in poor states like Mississippi, nearly flat in rich states like Connecticut
Does the relationship between education and vote choice differ across states too?

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Data: CES 2016

The 2016 Cooperative Congressional Election Study (Ansolabehere and Schaffner 2017; via Kuriwaki 2026)

A large (64,600 respondents) opt-in online survey run by YouGov
Respondents matched to state voter files.

Our sample: respondents with a validated vote record who say they voted for Clinton or Trump


ces <- read_csv("data/ces2016.csv") %>%
  mutate(college = as.integer(educ %in% c("BA", "Postgrad"))) # Has a 4-year degree
voters <- ces %>% filter(!is.na(clinton))


28,462 voters; Clinton won 65% of college graduates and 47% of everyone else

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Data: CES 2016

The “raw” education gap in each state: Clinton’s share among college graduates minus her share among non-graduates


raw_gaps <- voters %>% group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), gap = mean(clinton[college == 1]) - mean(clinton[college == 0]))



Is this variation real? Or is it noise from the small samples in small states?

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Complete pooling

Let’s start with a single logistic regression for everyone.

\(Y_{ij} = 1\) if respondent \(i\) in state \(j\) voted for Clinton, \(0\) if Trump.

\[Y_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij})\] \[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_{ij}}{1 - \pi_{ij}}\bigg) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{college}_{ij}\] \[\beta_0, \beta_1 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5^2)\]
Our only predictors are state and education, so every respondent in the same state \(\times\) education cell has the same \(\pi_{ij}\)

We’ll fit the model to all 28,462 respondents
But anything computed after estimation (predictions, model checks) only needs to be computed once for each of the 102 cells

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text: Diagnosing model fit

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Posterior predictive distribution

A very useful quantity to obtain is the predictive distribution of \(y\) given the model.
\[f(\tilde{y} | \mathbf{Y}) =\int f(\tilde{y}, \theta | \mathbf{Y}) d\theta = \int f(\tilde{y} | \mathbf{Y}, \theta) f(\theta | \mathbf{Y}) d\theta\]
Suppose our prediction target is the in-sample distribution of the covariates

We can get the posterior predictive distribution directly from our MCMC algorithm by drawing a value of \(y\) for each value of \(\theta\) that we sample.

(e.g.) for the logit

generated quantities {
  array[N] int y_rep = bernoulli_logit_rng(X * beta); //generate coin flips for each sample
}

It is common to use the posterior predictive distribution as a model diagnostic (“posterior predictive checking”)

Check in-sample fit: Does the model actually reproduce the distribution of the data?
Check against simulated data: Does the model recover the simulated distributions?

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Posterior predictive check

In our model, y_rep is a replicated count of Clinton voters for every cell

Drawing \(n_m\) Bernoulli outcomes with the same \(\pi_m\) and adding them up is the same as one Binomial(\(n_m\), \(\pi_m\)) draw

Our model should be able to reproduce Clinton’s share of the vote in each state


state_n <- tapply(cells$n, cells$state, sum) # Respondents per state
state_share_ppc <- function(fit){
  y_rep <- rstan::extract(fit, "y_rep")$y_rep # draws x cells
  share_rep <- sweep(t(rowsum(t(y_rep), cells$state)), 2, state_n, "/") # draws x states
  tibble(state = names(state_n), obs = tapply(cells$y, cells$state, sum)/state_n, mean = colMeans(share_rep),
         lower = apply(share_rep, 2, quantile, .025), upper = apply(share_rep, 2, quantile, .975))
}
ppc_pooled <- state_share_ppc(pooled_fit)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Varying intercepts model

Our regression from before is an example of a fully pooled regression.

Within individual states though, the regression line may be a poor predictor
The simplest fix is to allow the “intercept” to shift across units.

Assume:
\[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_{ij}}{1 - \pi_{ij}}\bigg) = X_{ij}^{\prime}\beta + \alpha_{j}\] \[\alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2_\alpha)\]
And keep the same prior as before on \(\beta\), which still contains the intercept. For \(\sigma_\alpha\) we’ll use a Half-Cauchy prior (a Cauchy with the constraint \(\sigma_\alpha > 0\)).
\(\alpha_j\) can be interpreted as the group-specific “shift” in the intercept from the “grand” intercept \(\beta_0\)

An equivalent parameterization would be to remove the intercept from \(\beta\) and write \(\alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_\alpha, \sigma^2_\alpha)\)

text:
Varying intercepts model

data{

  matrix[N, K] X; //matrix of covariates
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> y; // 1 = Clinton, 0 = Trump
  int J; // Number of groups
  array[N] int state; // group membership indicator
  int M; // number of cells
  matrix[M, K] X_cell; // covariates for each cell
  array[M] int n_cell; // number of respondents in each cell
  array[M] int cell_state; // group of each cell
}

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Model Diagnostics

There are two general approaches to evaluating model quality and comparing the predictive power of two or more statistical models given the same data

Information criteria
Cross-validation

Both approaches actually share common goals

Reward quality of predictions
Penalize model complexity

We want to avoid models that overfit to the observed data

Information criteria address this with an explicit penalty term for the number of parameters
Cross-validation methods do this by evaluating fit on a “held-out” part of the data that’s not used to estimate the model.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Information Criteria

Frequentist/MLE Inference - the Akaike Information Criterion
\[\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\ell(\hat{\theta})\]

\(k\) is the number of parameters and \(\ell(\hat{\theta})\) is the value of the maximized log-likelihood.
Pick the model with the lowest AIC

Bayesian Inference - the Deviance Information Criterion
\[\text{DIC} = 2p_{DIC} - 2\log p(y | \hat{\theta}_{\text{PM}})\]

\(\hat{\theta}_{\text{PM}}\) is the posterior mean and
the “effective number of parameters” is \(p_{DIC} = 2(\log p(y | \hat{\theta}_{\text{PM}}) - E_{\text{post}}[\log p(y|\theta)])\)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Log-predictive density

In general, a very common objective function for evaluating the quality of model “fit” in a Bayesian setting is the log-predictive density

Think of it as a more general version of criteria like “mean-squared error”

For a new “out-of-sample” \(\tilde{y}_i\), the log posterior predictive density is
\[\log p_{\text{post}} (\tilde{y}_i) = \log \int p(\tilde{y}_i | \theta) \times p_{\text{post}}(\theta)d\theta\]
We want to pick a model that has a high expected log pointwise-predictive density – for a “new” size \(n\) sample of observation drawn from a common distribution \(f(\tilde{y}_i)\),
\[\text{elppd} = \sum_{i=1}^n E_f[\log p_{\text{post}} (\tilde{y}_i)] = \sum_{i=1}^n\int \log p_{\text{post}} (\tilde{y}_i)f(\tilde{y}_i)d\tilde{y}_i\]
Our goal is to try to estimate this from the data that we have.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Estimating elppd

One approach would be to use the “in-sample” fit criterion using in-sample observations \(y_i\)
\[\text{lppd} = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_{\text{post}} (y_i)\]
We can calculate it by averaging over our \(S\) posterior samples
\[\widehat{\text{lppd}} = \sum_{i=1}^n \log \bigg( \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^S p(y_i | \theta^s)\bigg)\]
But here we know that it’s going to be biased (too optimistic) for the “out-of-sample” predictive accuracy due to over-fitting.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Estimating elppd

An improvement would be to correct the “in-sample” fit using a measure of the model complexity

This is the intuition behind AIC, DIC, (and other information criteria like WAIC)

An alternative would be to use cross-validation:

Split the sample into \(K\) “folds” (typical choice is 10)
For each fold \(k\), estimate the model on the \(K-1\) other folds
Using that model, calculate the log-predictive density for the observations in the \(k\)th fold
The \(k\)th fold is the “held-out” (or “test” set), the \(K-1\) remaining folds are the “training” set

When \(K = N\), this is often known as “leave-one out” cross-validation

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Leave-one-out CV

From Vehtari et al. (2017), our “leave-one-out” estimate of the expected log predictive density is:
\[\text{elpd}_{\text{loo}} = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(y_i | y_{-i})\]
In principle, this requires re-fitting the model to \(N\) datasets (with a single observation removed). However, it is possible to obtain an estimate of \(\log p(y_i | y_{-i})\) using the full model fit. Note:
\[p(y_i | y_{-i}) = \int p(y_i | \theta) p(\theta | y_{-i}) d\theta\]
We can calculate \(p(y_i | \theta)\) for a given draw of theta.

However, we only have draws from \(p(\theta | y)\) (our posterior).
The solution is to re-weight our draws such that, averaging over them yields an integral over \(p(\theta | y_{-i})\)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Leave-one-out CV

Ultimately, we need to re-weight by \(\frac{p(\theta_s | y_{-i})}{p(\theta_s | y)}\). Gelfand et al. (1992) show that under conditional independence in the model:
\[\frac{p(\theta_s | y_{-i})}{p(\theta_s | y)} =  \frac{p(\theta_s | y_{-i})}{p(\theta_s | y_i, y_{-i})} \propto \frac{p(\theta_s | y_{-i})}{p(y_i | \theta_s)p(\theta_s | y_{-i})} = \frac{1}{p(y_i | \theta_s)}\]
Let \(r^s_i = \frac{1}{p(y_i | \theta^s)}\) or the importance weight calculated for monte carlo sample \(s\)
Then our monte carlo estimate of \(p(y_i | y_{-i})\) is
\[p(y_i | y_{-i}) \approx \frac{\sum_{s=1}^S r_i^s p(y_i | \theta^s)}{\sum_{s=1}^S r_i^s}\]
Unfortunately, these importance weights are very poorly behaved (high variance).
Vehtari et al. (2017) propose an alternative method for estimating the importance weights: pareto-smoothed-importance-sampling (PSIS)

Fit a Pareto distribution to the upper tail of the importance ratios to stabilize the variance of the weights.

This PSIS-LOO cross-validation method is implemented in the loo R package.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Leave-one-out CV

For our example: \(N \times S\) is 28,462 respondents \(\times\) 8,000 draws \(\approx\) 228 million numbers (1.8 GB) for each model
So we’ll instead do the same calculation by state x education cell.

Every Clinton voter in cell \(m\) has the same log-likelihood, \(\log \pi_m\) (ll_clinton); every Trump voter has \(\log(1 - \pi_m)\) (ll_trump)
So they also have the same leave-one-out density
Run loo once for each cell \(\times\) vote, then replicate each result once per respondent who falls in that cell.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Leave-one-out CV

loo_respondents <- function(fit){
  # draws x chains x (cell, vote) combinations
  ll <- abind::abind(extract_log_lik(fit, "ll_clinton", merge_chains = F),
                     extract_log_lik(fit, "ll_trump", merge_chains = F), along = 3)
  loo_types <- loo(ll, r_eff = relative_eff(exp(ll)))
  rep(loo_types$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"], c(cells$y, cells$n - cells$y)) # one entry per respondent
}
elpd_summary <- function(pointwise) c(elpd_loo = sum(pointwise), se = sqrt(length(pointwise)*var(pointwise)))


loo_pooled <- loo_respondents(pooled_fit)
elpd_summary(loo_pooled)

Posterior predictive check

The varying intercepts model still assumes the same education gap (on the logit scale) in every state. Does it reproduce the gap in each state?


state_gap_ppc <- function(fit){
  y_rep <- rstan::extract(fit, "y_rep")$y_rep
  col <- cells$college == 1
  gap_rep <- sweep(y_rep[, col], 2, cells$n[col], "/") - sweep(y_rep[, !col], 2, cells$n[!col], "/")
  tibble(state = cells$state[col], obs = cells$y[col]/cells$n[col] - cells$y[!col]/cells$n[!col], mean = colMeans(gap_rep),
         lower = apply(gap_rep, 2, quantile, .025), upper = apply(gap_rep, 2, quantile, .975))
}

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Varying slopes model

What if we allow all of the parameters to vary by group?
\[\beta_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{\beta}, \Sigma_{\beta})\] \[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_{ij}}{1 - \pi_{ij}}\bigg) = X_{ij}^{\prime}\beta_{j}\]
This is a more general and flexible hierarchical model

But introduces a slight complication – we now need a prior distribution on an entire matrix \(\Sigma_{\beta}\) (the variances and covariances of the parameters).

The conjugate prior is the inverse-Wishart, the multivariate extension of the inverse-gamma.

An alternative non-conjugate prior (that appears to have better performance) is a scaled correlation matrix with an LKJ prior on the correlation matrix (see Stan documentation for more).
The latter is now preferred (especially by the Stan programmers)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Varying slopes model

Our prior on \(\Sigma_{\beta}\) starts by decomposing \(\Sigma_{\beta}\) into a diagonal scaling matrix \(\text{diag}(\tau)\) and a correlation matrix \(\Omega\)
\[\Sigma_{\beta} = \text{diag}(\tau)\Omega\text{diag}(\tau)\]
For each \(\tau_k\) we’ll use a Half-Cauchy distribution (Cauchy with the constraint \(\tau_k > 0\))
For \(\Omega\), we’ll use the Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe (LKJ) distribution which defines a distribution over correlation matrices

Intuition: Similar to a beta distribution in multiple dimensions.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Varying slopes model

Write each state’s coefficients as the national average plus a state-specific deviation
\[\beta_j = \mu_{\beta} + e_j, \qquad e_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \Sigma_{\beta})\] \[\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_{ij}}{1 - \pi_{ij}}\bigg) = \underbrace{X_{ij}^{\prime}\mu_{\beta}}_{\text{same in every state}} + \underbrace{X_{ij}^{\prime}e_j}_{\text{state deviation}}\]
Same setup as above, but keeping the part that’s the same in every state separate will make it easy to add state-level predictors later

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Varying slopes model

Add a second design matrix X_fix for the terms that are the same in every state (here, \(X_{ij}^{\prime}\mu_{\beta}\))

For now it’s just X again - but it will get more columns later



stan_data$P <- K
stan_data$X_fix <- X_mat
stan_data$X_fix_cell <- X_cell


Add them to the data block

  int P; // number of population-level coefficients
  matrix[N, P] X_fix; // population-level design matrix
  matrix[M, P] X_fix_cell; // population-level design matrix for each cell

                     model = colMeans(plogis(int_draws + slope_draws) - plogis(int_draws)))

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Group-level predictors

So far, every state’s coefficients are pooled towards the same national mean \(\mu_{\beta}\)

But we know a lot about the states themselves! (e.g. how they voted in 2012)

Let the mean of each state’s coefficients depend on a vector of \(L\) state-level predictors \(Z_j\) (including a 1 for the intercept)
\[\beta_j \sim \text{Normal}(\Gamma^{\prime}Z_j, \Sigma_{\beta})\]

\(\Gamma\) is an \(L \times K\) matrix: one column of coefficients for the state intercepts, one for the state slopes
Each state is pooled towards a prediction for that state rather than towards the national mean

Gelman et al. (2007) model the state intercepts and income slopes using each state’s average income and region

We’ll use Obama’s 2012 share of the state’s two-party vote (on the logit scale) and the state’s share of adults with a college degree (both standardized), so \(L = 3\)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Group-level predictors

As before, write each state’s coefficients as a mean plus a deviation: \(\beta_j = \Gamma^{\prime}Z_j + e_j\), with \(e_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \Sigma_{\beta})\)
Plug this into the linear predictor
\[\begin{aligned}\log\bigg(\frac{\pi_{ij}}{1 - \pi_{ij}}\bigg) = &\underbrace{(\Gamma_{11} + \Gamma_{21}\text{obama}_j + \Gamma_{31}\text{coll}_j + e_{0j})}_{\beta_{0j}\text{: intercept}} \\ &+ \underbrace{(\Gamma_{12} + \Gamma_{22}\text{obama}_j + \Gamma_{32}\text{coll}_j + e_{1j})}_{\beta_{1j}\text{: education slope}} \times \text{college}_{ij}\end{aligned}\]
The state-level predictors are just more regression terms

Main effects of \(\text{obama}_j\) and \(\text{coll}_j\) (shifting the intercepts), plus their interactions with \(\text{college}_{ij}\) (shifting the slopes)
Plus the same zero-mean state deviations \(e_j\) as in the varying slopes model

                                           state_college = as.numeric(scale(college_share)))
X_fix <- model.matrix(~ college * (state_obama + state_college), data = voters %>% left_join(state_preds_z, by = "state"))

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Group-level predictors

Once we know a state’s 2012 vote, the states don’t differ by much more: the \(\tau\)’s are close to zero

That’s a hard posterior for the sampler: when \(\tau\) is small, the \(e_j\)’s are squeezed into a narrow “funnel”
With the default settings, we get some divergent transitions

An easy fix is to raise adapt_delta so the “leapfrog” solver takes smaller steps

The divergences go away, but the \(\tau\)’s have small effective sample sizes (lots of autocorrelation from small steps)
brms avoids the problem by reparameterizing the model (more later)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Multilevel Regression and Post-stratification

Often we’re interested in estimating political attitudes at very small areas

Within a nationally-representative sample, we may only have a minor fraction of respondents who are even in a particular region.

Beyond that, our sample may not be demographically representative for a given region

Can we do better than just using the sub-group means for our outcome of interest?

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
MrP

Multilevel Regression and Post-stratification combines two well-known tools to try to accomplish this task (Park et al. 2004)

Multilevel regression: Using the entire dataset, specify a flexible model for the outcome of interest
Post-stratification: Using known population characteristics, generate predictions for each covariate “cell” in each region

The national-level regression allows us to improve precision in small-area estimation

e.g. if some of the variability between regions is driven by individual or group-level characteristics, we can model the relationship between those characteristics and the outcome using all the data.

The population-level data allows us to address non-response/sampling bias

Ideally all of the variables that would go in the survey weighting model also go in the MrP model (so in principle we don’t need to include survey weights in the analysis)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
MrP Workflow

Get survey data that contains individual and group-level predictors (e.g. demographic characteristics + “small area” of residence)
Get information on the “small areas” themselves
Estimate a multilevel regression model using these two sets of data
Construct a post-stratification frame that has the joint distribution of our demographics for each “small area”
Predict using the model for each cell in the post-stratification frame
Aggregate to get predictions for each small area

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Post-stratification

The easiest approach to adjusting a non-representative survey is to weight to match the known joint distribution of \(x\) in the population \(f_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{x})\)

This requires a lot of auxiliary information about the target - typically obtained from high-quality census data
(e.g.) U.S. Census Public-Use Microdata: What is the share of Black, college educated, 30-45 year olds in Massachusetts?

In post-stratification, we divide our sample up into \(C\) cells \(c\) that are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

\(\tilde{T}_{\mathbf{x}} = \{\tilde{P}_{1}, \tilde{P}_2, \dotsc, \tilde{P}_{C}\}\) is our population distribution of these cells

Our sampling/response model assumes that within each of these cells we have a simple-random sample from that particular stratum of the population

There may be variation in non-response or over/under-sampling, but only across cells
“post”-stratification because the intuition is akin to a design where we actually did stratify ex-ante

Our measurement model assumes we observe the joint distribution of auxiliary variables \(\mathbf{x}\) in the target population

Difficult in many cases!

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Post-stratification

Two ways to think of post-stratification:
First - Let \(\hat{\theta}_{y}^{c}\) denote our estimator for the population mean within cell \(c\)

Then, our post-stratification estimator \(\hat{\theta}_{y}^{PS}\) is:

\[\hat{\theta}_{y}^{PS} = \sum_{c=1}^C \tilde{P}_{c} \hat{\theta}_{y}^{c}\]
Alternatively, we’ll sometimes write \(\tilde{P}_c = \frac{\tilde{N}_c}{\tilde{N}}\) where \(\tilde{N}\) is the size of the population and \(\tilde{N}_c\) is the number of units in that cell.
\[\hat{\theta}_{y}^{PS} = \sum_{c=1}^C \frac{\tilde{N}_c}{\tilde{N}} \hat{\theta}_{y}^{c}\]
Fixed “constant” weights on the within-cell estimators.

This is how we’ll approach it with MRP.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Post-stratification

Second - We can think of it as weighting individual observations using our adjustment weights \(\tilde{w}^{PS}_i\)

This is more common in survey weighting approaches to balancing sample and population.

Let \(c(i)\) denote the class to which unit \(i\) belongs. Then the post-stratification weights are
\[\tilde{w}^{PS}_i = (\tilde{P}_{c(i)}/\hat{P}^{S}_{c(i)}) \times d_i\]
where \(\hat{P}^{S}_{c(i)}\) is the estimated in-sample proportion of observations in class \(c\) and \(d_i\) is unit \(i\)’s design weight
When design weights are constant, \(\hat{P}^{S}_{c(i)}\) is just the sample mean of the indicator of class membership \(\mathbf{1}(i \in c)\)

More generally, you can write it as \(\hat{P}^{S}_{c(i)} = (\sum_{i=1}^N  d_i \mathbf{1}(i \in c))/(\sum_{i=1}^N d_i)\)

Intuition

The weights up-weight observations that are under-represented in the sample relative to the target population
The weights down-weight observations that are over-represented in the sample relative to the target population.

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Example: CES 2016

How well does the unweighted CES do at estimating Clinton’s share of the two-party vote in each state? (Actual county returns from MIT Election Data and Science Lab (2018))


pres <- read_csv("data/county_pres_2012_2016.csv")
state_results <- pres %>% group_by(state) %>% summarize(actual = sum(dem_2016)/sum(dem_2016 + rep_2016))
state_raw <- voters %>% group_by(state) %>% summarize(n = n(), raw = mean(clinton)) %>%
  inner_join(state_results, by = "state") # Alaska doesn't report results by county

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Example: CES 2016

Let’s fit a regression model

We’ll use the brms package which has pre-existing implementations of popular models like the random slopes/random intercepts generalized linear mixed model

We’ll fit a logistic regression with coefficients on gender, age and college degree as well as our varying intercepts and education slopes by state

The brms formula syntax: (1 + college | state) is our varying slopes model from before



library(brms)


vote_cells <- voters %>% group_by(state, female, age, college) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), clinton = sum(clinton), .groups = "drop")


state_mlm <- brm(clinton | trials(n) ~ female + age + college + (1 + college | state),
                 family = binomial, data = vote_cells, cores = 4, seed = 53706, refresh = 0)

text:
Who is the target population?

Our post-stratification frame comes from the Census - it counts adults

But our target is Clinton’s share among voters
Turnout differs a lot across cells (e.g. by age and education)

So we need a second model: the probability that someone in each cell turns out

We can fit it on the whole CES sample, voters and non-voters (validated turnout)
Then weight each cell by \(\tilde{N}_c \times \Pr(\text{vote} | c)\)

  summarize(n = n(), voted = sum(voted), .groups = "drop")


turnout_mlm <- brm(voted | trials(n) ~ female + age + college + (1 | state),
                   family = binomial, data = turnout_cells, cores = 4, seed = 53706, refresh = 0)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Predicting with the model

Our models only depend on state and demographics: predict once for each state x gender x age x college degree cell


state_frame <- acs %>% group_by(state, female, age, college) %>%
  summarize(N = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(n = 1) # n = 1: predict a probability

state_frame$p_clinton <- colMeans(posterior_epred(state_mlm, newdata = state_frame))

mrp_states <- state_frame %>% group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(mrp = sum(N * p_turnout * p_clinton)/sum(N * p_turnout)) %>%
  inner_join(state_raw, by = "state")

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
section: Pitfall: Pooling towards the national mean
text:
Pitfall: Pooling towards the national mean

MrP barely reduces the average bias, and its RMSE is worse than the raw means

The state intercepts are partially pooled towards a common grand mean
So the most extreme states get pulled towards the middle

DC: raw 97%, MrP 78%, actual 96%
Wyoming: raw 48%, MrP 50%, actual 24%
But we know there are some extreme states out there!

The solution is to include state-level predictors (e.g. past vote share), so that each state is pooled towards a prediction for that state, not towards the nation as a whole (Park et al. 2004)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Group-level predictors in brms

In brms (and lme4), a group-level predictor is just a population-level term: a column that’s constant within each group
y ~ college * (state_obama + state_college) + (1 + college | state)









Term
Role
In \(\Gamma\)




1, college
national average intercept and education slope
\(\Gamma_{11}, \Gamma_{12}\)


state_obama, state_college
shift the state intercepts
\(\Gamma_{21}, \Gamma_{31}\)


college:state_obama, college:state_college
shift the state education slopes
\(\Gamma_{22}, \Gamma_{32}\)


(1 + college \| state)
zero-mean state deviations
\(e_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \Sigma_{\beta})\)




This is exactly our model from before, (though brms has slightly different default priors)

Mechanically, brms also avoids divergent transitions by not sampling \(\tau\) directly (a “non-centered” parameterization)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Group-level predictors in brms

Only the interactions move the slopes: main effects of the state-level predictors shift the intercepts
Every varying term needs a population-level counterpart

(1 + college | state) centers the state slopes at zero, so college has to be in the population-level part too
Otherwise we’re assuming that the average education gap is zero

Merge the group-level predictors onto every row of the data (they must be constant within each group - brms won’t check!)
This works with varying intercepts, but not with state fixed effects

With a dummy for each state, state_obama would be perfectly collinear with the dummies
With partially pooled intercepts, its coefficient is learned from the differences between states

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
Group-level predictors in brms

brms can also write the model literally as \(\beta_j = \Gamma^{\prime}Z_j + e_j\) with its bf() formula syntax


bf(clinton | trials(n) ~ b0 + b1 * college,
   b0 ~ state_obama + state_college + (1 | s | state), # intercepts: Gamma[, 1] + e_0j
   b1 ~ state_obama + state_college + (1 | s | state), # slopes: Gamma[, 2] + e_1j
   nl = TRUE) # the shared "s" lets e_0j and e_1j be correlated


Here we’ll stick with the formula version. Add the state-level predictors to our cells


vote_cells_st <- vote_cells %>% left_join(state_preds_z, by = "state")


state_mlm2 <- brm(clinton | trials(n) ~ female + age + college * (state_obama + state_college) +
                    (1 + college | state),
                  family = binomial, data = vote_cells_st, cores = 4, seed = 53706, refresh = 0)

In the model, the only thing that distinguishes two counties in the same state is their demographics (gender, age, education)

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
County-level predictors

The solution is to give the model information about the small areas themselves

A county-level predictor: Obama’s 2012 share of the two-party vote in the county (on the logit scale)
A varying intercept for each county, partially pooled towards the prediction from the county-level predictor

In brms, a group-level predictor is just another column that’s constant within each group: obama_2012 + (1 | county_fips) pools each county’s intercept towards \(\gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \times \text{(2012 vote)}_c\)
The county’s own 2012 vote takes the place of the state-level predictors

Counties with no respondents still get a prediction from their demographics, their state, and their 2012 vote



county_info <- pres %>% transmute(county_fips, obama_2012 = qlogis(dem_share_2012))
county_cells <- voters %>% inner_join(county_info, by = "county_fips") %>%
  group_by(state, county_fips, obama_2012, female, age, college) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), clinton = sum(clinton), .groups = "drop")


county_mlm <- brm(clinton | trials(n) ~ female + age + college + obama_2012 +
                    (1 + college | state) + (1 | county_fips),
                  family = binomial, data = county_cells, cores = 4, seed = 53706, refresh = 0)

  summarize(mrp_county = sum(n_adults * p_turnout * p_clinton)/sum(n_adults * p_turnout)) %>%

mrp_states %>% pivot_longer(c(raw, mrp, mrp_statepred, mrp_county), names_to = "estimate") %>% group_by(estimate) %>%
  summarize(rmse = sqrt(mean((value - actual)^2)), bias = mean(value - actual))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  estimate        rmse   bias
  <chr>          <dbl>  <dbl>
1 mrp           0.0865 0.0488
2 mrp_county    0.0595 0.0461
3 mrp_statepred 0.0681 0.0485
4 raw           0.0774 0.0518

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
section: MrP can only fix what’s in the model
text:
MrP can only fix what’s in the model

Even with the county predictor, our estimates still lean towards Clinton

Clinton’s estimated share is 4.6 points too high in the average state, and 8.5 points too high in the average county

The sampling/response model assumption: within each cell, respondents look like non-respondents

CES respondents are more Democratic than people with the same gender, age, education and county who didn’t take the survey

title: Week 7: Multilevel Models
text:
How to improve this model

We’ve provided a very simple example of an MrP model but there are a lot of ways it can be improved

More group-level predictors (e.g. county demographics, urbanicity)
Individual-level interactions in the model + partial-pooling on the coefficients
More covariates + knowing the true joint distribution in the population.
Many more possibilities…

MrP is most powerful when there are very few respondents from a particular small area in our data

But it can only correct for differences between the sample and the population that are in the model
